title: A Self-hosted Deferred Deep linking. Firebase dynamic link model
description: Self-hosted deferred deep linking and referral attribution for React Native. An open-source replacement for the deferred-linking half of Firebase Dynamic Links — Android Install Referrer, iOS clipb...
fullText:
A deferred deep linking referral system you fork and self-host: four
packages — two interchangeable backends, plus web and mobile — and runnable
examples. In production at Sparkle, a Nigerian
microfinance bank. New here? Read this file top to bottom — it's
written as a guided path, not a reference dump: what this is, how it works,
how to run it, and where to go next depending on what you're trying to do.

A referral link tapped on a real iPhone, on cellular, installing from the
App Store — and the code arriving in the signup field on the other side.
This isn't the demo app or a staged build: it's
Sparkle's live production release, a Nigerian
microfinance bank, running this SDK.

Thirty-five seconds, one take, nothing sped up or cut:

That half-second is the entire point of the iOS deterministic tier. The
code was written to the clipboard by the landing page moments before the
App Store redirect, survived the install, and came back without a network
call, a fingerprint guess, or the user typing anything.

Two details worth watching for, because both are deliberate:

This is the iOS path, which is the harder one to believe — it depends on a
clipboard payload surviving Safari, the App Store and an install. Android
is the easy case and needs no video: the Play Install Referrer hands the
code over before the app's first frame.

Want to drive it yourself rather than watch? Quick start
has a live web demo and an Android APK.

Deterministic and probabilistic recovery are two separate mechanisms, not
two branches of one path — shown below as two diagrams, both starting at
the same click and ending at the same claim.

Android's default path, and iOS's opt-in path — both read a code and proof
entirely on-device, no network call. Neither touches fingerprint matching
at all.

Reached only when the deterministic path above didn't run or didn't have
anything to read — a scored guess, backed by the same signed token once it
succeeds. Both platforms feed the same scoring engine; this is the one
piece of matching logic that isn't platform-specific at all.

Reliability: Android deterministic recovery hits ~100% of real
installs; iOS deterministic recovery depends entirely on whether the paste
button is rendered and tapped. Probabilistic matching sees an observed
~85–90% match rate on iOS, where it's the default fallback; lower priority
on Android, where it's a fallback of last resort.

Treat that iOS figure as what a single self-hosted deployment sees, and
don't compare it directly against a commercial MMP's published numbers.
Branch and AppsFlyer score probabilistic matches against signal pooled
across their whole SDK install base — many apps, shared IP graphs — while
this only ever sees your own clicks. That's a structural difference in
available signal, not a tuning gap you can close by adjusting weights.

The proof that makes both deterministic paths possible: every
recovered code carries a signed proof (click_id.expiry.hmac), minted
once at /click — this is what lets both deterministic paths stay
genuinely network-free at recovery time, and what /claim verifies before
any reward is paid out. A code with no valid token behind it (including
one a user typed in by hand) can reach signup, but can never clear
/claim — see docs/decisions.md #21/#22 for the
full reasoning behind why this replaced an earlier redeem-round-trip
design.

Read the scope line first, because it's the part that decides whether
this is for you: Branch and AppsFlyer are mobile measurement platforms.
blynk-deferlink is the deferred-deep-linking and referral-attribution
slice of what they do, self-hosted. If you need ad-network attribution,
this is not a replacement.

Worth being blunt about, because it's most of what the money buys:

When to use them instead: you're running paid acquisition and need
MMP attribution; you want fraud protection you don't have to build; or
you'd rather buy a supported product than operate one. Those are good
reasons, and this project doesn't pretend otherwise.

When to use this: referral and invite flows are the attribution you
care about, you want the data in your own database, or a per-MAU bill
doesn't make sense for your margins.

FDL was deprecated in May 2023 with no official replacement and shut
down completely on 25 August 2025 — every link stopped resolving,
deferred linking included. If that's what brought you here, this is
probably a closer fit than Branch is.

FDL was never an MMP. It did link hosting, Universal/App Links handling,
deferred deep linking, and basic click analytics — and nothing else. No
ad-network attribution, no fraud detection, no campaign analytics. So the
honest mapping is:

In other words: this covers the deferred-attribution half of FDL, not
the link-hosting half. That's the honest scope. If all you needed was the
deferred part — which for referral flows is usually the case — the gap is
smaller than it looks, and you get to keep the data.

Running in production at Sparkle, a Nigerian
microfinance bank, on the PHP backend — real referral traffic, real
conversions. A second Sparkle app is rolling out on it now. The Node
backend serves this project's own live demo.

See it live in production: https://sparkle.ng/referral/L82WDL — a real
Sparkle referral link, served by this SDK. Open it on a phone to watch the
actual flow: the landing page registers a click, hands the code off, and
the app recovers it after install. (It's the maintainer's own referral
link — Sparkle only credits a referral once a referred user completes a
first transaction, so opening it to watch the mechanics does nothing. It's
here because a real production link demonstrates more than a staged one.)

One thing worth knowing: coverage is uneven by package. The scoring
engine, click tokens and conversion tracking are well covered on both
backends; referral-web's test suite is new and still thin. CI runs every
suite on each PR across both Node and PHP version ranges.

docs/decisions.md is the honest record of how this was built — including
the bugs found by actually running it on real devices, and the trade-offs
accepted rather than solved. It's the fastest way to judge whether the
engineering here meets your bar.

Don't want to clone anything yet? Try the recovery flow live
— pick a referral code and it builds a real link to the actual production
landing page (real countdown, real click registration, real clipboard
handoff), then recovers it exactly how a real installed app would (Android:
automatic via the Play referrer param; iOS: a real clipboard check, falling
back to a real fingerprint match), with the actual request/response for
every step.

Want the real mobile app, not just the web half? Download the Android
demo APK
— open that link on an Android device and install it; no Play Store
listing and no Expo account needed. You'll have to allow installs from
your browser the first time, since it's unlisted rather than
Play-distributed. It's served from a GitHub
release
deliberately: the EAS build link this used to point at expires after 30
days, and did — a release asset doesn't. iOS has no equivalent link —
internal distribution there needs a registered Apple Developer account and
per-device UDID registration, so for now the iOS side is only reachable by
building it yourself (see below), or by watching it run in production in
See it working above.

Otherwise, the fastest way to see the whole thing work locally, before
installing anything for real. Three terminals. No PHP or database required
— the mock backend covers it.

Open the web page with ?code=1234 and watch the backend log the click. On
desktop it shows both store buttons; on a phone browser it attempts the app
handoff then redirects to the store.

The mobile app recovers automatically on launch, same as a real app —
there's nothing to simulate inside it. To see it actually find something,
type a code into its own "Generate a referral link" card and tap Open
link — that opens the real landing page in your device/simulator's
browser (real countdown, real click registration, real clipboard handoff),
then switch back to the app to see the recovery.

Once the demo makes sense, this is where to go depending on what you're
actually trying to do:

Setting this up for real — pick the piece you need:

The four recovery paths (deterministic/probabilistic × Android/iOS),
diagrammed, live in How it works above rather than a
separate doc — it's central enough to the project to read before anything
else, not something to click away for.

Understanding why it's built this way, not just how to use it:
docs/decisions.md — the engineering-decisions log.
Every non-obvious choice in this codebase (why matching uses a graduated
recency score, why /claim requires a signed token instead of trusting the
request, why the mobile SDK persists nothing to disk) is written up there
with the problem it solved, in chronological order.

API/config reference for a package you've already set up lives in that
package's own README (packages/*/README.md) — the integration guides above
are the walkthrough; the READMEs are what to come back to for a specific
config field or endpoint shape.

Fork it and run it as your own. That's the intended model, not a
temporary state of affairs. Attribution data is the thing you least want
sitting behind someone else's API: every click, every device fingerprint,
every conversion. Self-hosting means the click table lives in your
database, the matching runs on your server, and nobody can reprice,
rate-limit, sunset, or read it. Firebase Dynamic Links shut down in August
2025 and took every link with it; that risk is the whole reason this
exists, and shipping it as a hosted dependency would just recreate it.

So there's no registry install. Fork or clone, point the backend at your
database, and change whatever doesn't fit — the code is yours at that
point, and the API contract is small enough to modify without fear (two
independent backends implement it, which is the proof it's not tangled).

The full reasoning, including what this costs you — slower to adopt than
npm install, and forks get no automatic security updates — is
decision #31.

This is how it runs in production today. Sparkle, a
Nigerian microfinance bank, runs its referral programme on it: the PHP
backend SDK deployed on their own infrastructure, against their own
database and their own reward logic. Nothing in this repo is a staging
copy of that — it's the same code path, which is why the bugs in
docs/decisions.md were found on real devices rather
than in tests.

The packages are consumed from source. Three ways, depending on how your
project is laid out:

1. Workspaces (what this repo uses). From the repo root:

The examples already declare the SDKs as file: dependencies, so they resolve
to the local source automatically.

2. A file: dependency in your own project.

React Native's Metro bundles the SDK straight from its TypeScript source (the
package's react-native field points at src/), so no build step is needed for
the mobile SDK. The web SDK is consumed from source here via a Vite alias; for a
non-source consumer, build it first (below).

3. A tarball. Build, pack, then install the .tgz anywhere:

Publishing your fork privately. If your team would rather consume these
as ordinary dependencies than as source, publish them to your own registry
under your own scope: npm run build:sdks, then npm publish in each
package, and composer / Packagist for the PHP one. Renaming the scope in
each package.json is the only change required.

Contributions are genuinely welcome, and the project is set up so that a
first one is easy to land.

CONTRIBUTING.md covers setup, how to run each
package's tests, and what to verify before opening a PR. CI runs every
suite on each PR across both Node and PHP version ranges, so you get
automated feedback without waiting on a review.

title: ‘RAMageddon’: tech crunch hikes the price of your next iPhone by £100

fullText:
Shortage of memory chips and other critical components reverses trend of electronics becoming cheaper

Apple’s recent product launch caused headlines around the world as it unveiled its first folding phone. But hidden in the slick technology showcase was a nasty surprise: a £100 increase in the price of all iPhones, including older models.

It is blamed on “RAMageddon”, which has reversed a decades-long trend of electronics becoming cheaper. It is the fallout from the AI gold rush hoovering up every memory chip available for vast datacentres. This has led to a severe shortage of the chips, and other critical components, for electronics, including phones.

The situation has dramatically driven up costs, with some chips five times dearer than previously listed. Therefore the everyday electronics products people rely on are suddenly significantly more expensive to make, and that is being passed on to consumers.

“Two things are happening at once,” says Francisco Jeronimo, the vice-president of client devices at research company IDC. “Component costs have risen sharply, with memory alone up more than 300% year on year.”

Because older iPhones use the same expensive memory as the new ones, Apple is pricing them as current products, he adds.

The iPhone is not the first product to have a “RAMageddon” price increase, but it is the single biggest-selling electrical product in the world. For many, this means the real cost of the AI splurge will be £100 without getting anything more for your money.

Other manufacturers of smartphones have also increased the price of new models, with Samsung and Google adding up to £80 to their flagship phones.

Apple has also increased the price of its refurbished stock by £60 to £70, including the older iPhone 15 that is no longer sold new in the shops. However, according to data from Uswitch, the increase in cost has yet to reach the third-party refurbished iPhone market.

“A refurbished iPhone 16 has held at about £503 all summer, roughly where it was before the 18 Pro launch,” says Ernest Doku, a Uswitch mobiles expert. “A refurbished 14 is about £10 cheaper than it was in June, while the 16 has simply stopped falling in price.”

Most smartphone makers, other than Apple, have discontinued older models that were no longer economically viable, and likely wouldn’t sell at higher prices. The impact has been particularly acute at the lower end of the market.

In its latest forecast, IDC predicts there will be the steepest annual contraction in worldwide smartphone sales on record this year, falling almost 17% to just over 1bn handsets. “People are buying fewer phones and paying considerably more for those they do buy,” Jeronimo says.

There have been bigger price rises for other electronics. Computer makers, which are much more exposed to rapidly jumping memory and chip costs, have had to raise prices several times over the past 18 months.

Microsoft added up to £220 to some of its Surface computers but also released versions with half as much memory as a way to attempt to keep prices down.

The move has forced the company to try to redesign Windows to run more comfortably with only 8GB of RAM, which it hasn’t for several years.

Many of PC maker Dell’s high-end laptops have jumped by as much as 25%, while the repairable laptop maker Framework has had to continually adjust prices as costs fluctuate.

Even Apple added £100 to its lower-cost MacBook Neo, as well as rises to most models in its Mac and iPad lines in June. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” the company says in a statement.

Games consoles aren’t immune, either. In a rare state of affairs, Microsoft recently increased the price of its near six-year-old console to £670, up from its original launch price of £449.

“Console storage and memory prices have increased by more than 2.5 times, and we expect another doubling by the autumn of 2027,” the company says.

Unfortunately, £100 added to the cost of a phone may only be the start of the price pain, with key memory producers, including SK Hynix, suggesting the shortages could last beyond 2030.

Jeronimo says memory prices are going to continue rising well into 2027, even if the pace has slowed from the “extraordinary spikes” seen earlier this year. “Even once memory costs ease, I do not expect smartphone prices to fall back to the same levels as last year.

“Increases in this industry tend to be sticky. Once customers have absorbed a higher price and manufacturers have rebuilt their margins, companies hold the line and add value through storage or features, rather than cutting the ticket price.”

The bad news for consumers is that “the era of cheap smartphones – or any device to be honest – is over,” Jeronimo says.

title: How to Claim Your Piece of Apple's $250 Million Siri Settlement
description: If you bought an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16, you may be eligible for a payout.
fullText:
Last week, Apple released Siri AI, the company's biggest overhaul to its smart assistant ever. If you have a compatible device running the latest updates, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, you now have access to Apple's AI-powered Siri, in addition to a number of new Apple Intelligence features. For some of us, this might seem like a welcome upgrade from a company that hasn't done as much with AI as its competitors. For others, it's a long overdue fulfillment of a promise. So overdue, in fact, that Apple may be offering a payout to make up for it.

This year's iOS updates aren't the first we've seen of Siri AI. Back in 2024, Apple advertised a new AI-powered Siri that could understand content on your screen and pull data from your various apps to inform its answers. In Apple's pre-recorded demos, for example, Siri could dive through your texts and emails to locate a family member's travel information if you asked the assistant what time that person's flight arrived. Apple said this new Siri would arrive with iOS 18 later that year, launching on compatible iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 devices. But while the company slowly rolled out Apple Intelligence features through the iOS 18 lifecycle, this new Siri was nowhere to be found.

For many, this absence ranged from mildly humorous to frustrating. Some, however, found it deceptive. After all, Apple said users who bought a certain iPhone could expect it to run this supercharged Siri. You might have picked up an iPhone 16, or perhaps the previous-generation iPhone 15 Pro, assuming you could take advantage of Apple's AI-powered assistant, but those changes didn't actually arrive until last week, more than two years after Apple first announced them. Depending on your upgrade cycle, you could be on your second or third smartphone since then.

These grievances weren't confined to grousing on the internet. The Clarkson law firm filed a suit against Apple, alleging the company misled customers with these new Siri features. While the company has not admitted wrongdoing, it did agree to a $250 million settlement to put the case aside. And if you're eligible, it is now time to claim your share of the settlement.

Not all iPhone owners are eligible for a slice of this settlement. Per the terms, only customers who bought an iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model (iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 16e) can claim a share. What's more, there's a specific timeline during which purchases are eligible: June 10, 2024, to March 29, 2025.

If you bought your iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 between these dates, you can make a claim. To start, head to the settlement's official website, then choose "File A Claim." If you have a Claim ID and PIN, you can share them here. If you don't, you can still choose to file a claim online. You can share your iPhone's serial number, though if you don't have it, you can share your Apple Account email address and the number associated with your iPhone. Claims are open from today, Sept. 21, through Dec. 21.

While $250 million sounds like a huge payout, the final amount likely won't be: The estimated payout is $25 per claimant, though that may change depending on the number of respondents. If there are fewer claims than expected, you may receive as much as $95. As MacRumors reports, the final approval hearing is on Feb. 24 of next year, so don't expect the money any time soon.

title: 10 Keyboard Hacks Every iPhone User Should Know
description: These hacks help you make the most of typing on your iPhone.
fullText:
On the surface, the iPhone keyboard looks like it did a decade ago, but underneath, much has changed. In addition to the hidden features that have existed for years, Apple has slowly added features and gestures that make typing a bit easier. If you're still shaking your iPhone to undo text, it's time to dig deeper. These 10 hacks can help you make the most of typing on your iPhone.

Typing on an iPhone’s glass surface can feel a bit lifeless, especially if you’re used to typing on mechanical keyboards on your Mac. While there’s no way to get a physical keyboard on the iPhone (unless you get something like the Clicks keyboard), you can simulate it. The iPhone has a built-in Taptic engine, which provides subtle vibrations as you interact with the device. While most know it from notifications, calls, and scrolling through various iOS UI elements, it can be enabled for the keyboard too. Go to Settings > Sounds & Haptics > Keyboard Feedback and enable \"Haptic Feedback."

When you type on the iPhone keyboard, all you see are letters. To type numbers or symbols, you have to switch to the “123” keyboard layout instead—unless you use this hidden gesture, that is. See, each letter is already hiding a number or alternative symbol behind it. All you need to do to reveal it is to swipe from the 123 key. Once you do that, the keyboard will reveal numbers and symbols. Drag your finger to the number you want to enter, let go, and it’s done. The keyboard goes back to being a keyboard.

The iPhone has OCR (optical character recognition) built into iOS. You use this anytime you copy text from an image in the Photos app. The same feature is integrated into the Camera app, and lets you paste that text straight into any field, bypassing the keyboard entirely. To do so, point the camera towards any text, and the app will frame it in a yellow border. You’ll also see a Live Text button in the bottom-right corner. Tap on it, select the text, and tap the Copy button. Now, open any text field, and you’ll see a suggestion to paste the text you just copied.

If you have a large iPhone, typing with one hand can be extremely difficult. Instead, use the keyboard's one-handed mode. Tap and hold the Globe key to find options to dock the one-handed keyboard to the left or the right (below the list of all available keyboards). If you don’t see it, go to Settings > General > Keyboard > One-Handed Keyboard and choose Left or Right from here. Once enabled, you’ll see a shrunken keyboard layout docked to one side of the screen. Tap the Arrow button to change the docking position. Unfortunately, unlike Gboard on Android, you can’t resize the keyboard itself, but this does make it much easier to use your keyboard with one hand.

Apple’s built-in Text Replacement feature can transform a couple of pre-programmed letters into canned responses. That could be your address, an email template for clients, a signature, a repeated sign-off message, anything you frequently type. Go to Settings > General > Keyboard > Text Replacement. Here, tap the Plus button from the top, add the expanded response in the "Phrase" field and the trigger characters in the "Shortcut" field.

You can simply drag the iPhone’s cursor to select text. But instead of fiddling with the little cursor point, try tapping on the screen. You can double-tap a word to quickly select it; triple-tap, and you’ll select the sentence. Tap four times, and now the entire paragraph is selected.

Once you’ve selected the text, pinch in with three fingers to quickly copy the text. Pinch outwards with three fingers to paste the text. You can also swipe left with three fingers to undo anything you just did. For precise text selection, nothing beats the trackpad hack. You might already know that if you press and hold the Space bar on the iPhone keyboard, the whole thing turns into a trackpad. But you can also use this feature to select text. Keep your finger on the Space bar, but use another finger to move the cursor to select the text.

There may be times when the iPhone keyboard goes haywire. Autocorrect might keep suggesting words you never type, or it keeps bringing up specific casual words you type in a group chat, but don’t mean to repeat. If you’re fed up with keyboard suggestions, there is an out. You can reset the whole thing, starting fresh by rebuilding the suggestions library. Go to Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Reset > Reset Keyboard Dictionary to get started.

If you’re multilingual, you might constantly switch between keyboards to type in your target language. Now, you don't need to do that. You can enable multilingual support to type in different languages on a single keyboard. When you enable two languages, the iPhone keyboard adapts automatically. It knows which language you’re typing and will even provide different suggestions based on it. Go to Settings > General > Keyboard > Keyboards > Add New Keyboard. Choose a language, and then select if you want to add a new keyboard, or if you want to add the language to your existing keyboard.

You shouldn’t trust AI to write for you, but you can use it to proofread and edit text you’ve crafted yourself. And there’s no need to pay for an AI subscription either. If you have Apple Intelligence built into your iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro and later), you can use the Writing Tools feature instead. Writing Tools is integrated into the Notes app, Mail app, and basically anywhere you write text. Select the text, and from the pop-up menu, choose "Writing Tools." From here, ask Siri to make the text shorter, format it to make it sound more formal, and, of course, to check for grammar and spelling mistakes.

title: This New iOS 27 Feature May Save You From Getting Scammed
description: It's designed to detect and prevent social engineering scams.
fullText:
Starting with iOS 27, your iPhone now has a built-in scam prevention feature, designed to protect you from social engineering scams. These scams rely on pressure tactics to trick you into bypassing security features for your phone, laptop, or online accounts. Here's how iOS 27's "Impersonation Risk Detection" works, what it can do, and its current limitations.

In a social engineering scam, a bad actor impersonates an official rep of a bank, government agency, or a tech company such as Apple, Google, or Microsoft. The scammer may even impersonate your friends, family members, or colleagues you trust. They'll try to force you to disable account security measures such as two-factor authentication, or talk you into sharing your financial information. They'll create a fake problem, establish trust, and then pressure you into making large payments.

Apple says Impersonation Risk Detection can analyze information about your iPhone or iPad, your Apple Account, and check for signs of an active scam. Once it completes the analysis, iOS 27 will share a risk level with the app that's being targeted by scammers. Apple emphasizes that the app doesn't receive any data associated with your device or Apple Account that was used to assess the risk level.

From there, it's up to the app to decide how to proceed. If an app supports Impersonation Risk Detection, it may add a delay to each step you're trying to execute, show warnings, or even ask you to verify your identity. Apps can use various factors to decide if they need a risk assessment from iOS 27, which include big changes to your account, resetting its password, disabling two-factor authentication, making large payments, etc.

Once an app requests iOS 27 for a risk assessment, the operating system can conduct an analysis and place the action into one of three risk level markers (again, Apple doesn't control what apps do with the risk level information):

Unknown: This means that iOS 27 couldn't detect any suspicious activity. Apple says that doesn't mean the action was confirmed as safe.

Medium: This risk level is assigned when iOS 27 detects some signs of suspicious activity.

High: This risk level is associated with significant signs of suspicious activity.

Once you've updated your iPhone to iOS 27 (or your iPad to iPadOS 27), go to Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll to the bottom, and tap Impersonation Risk Detection. Enable the toggle next to "Share with App Developers." Now, tap Share with App Developers in the pop-up. Once Impersonation Risk Detection is enabled, you don't need to take further action. Note that when you try to disable this feature, it may take up to 24 hours to take effect. This is to protect you from scammers, who may pressure you into disabling the feature.

In the same settings page, you'll be able to see which app requested access to your risk levels, and why. This will show up under the "Recent Activity" section. You'll also be able to turn off this feature for individual apps that appear in this section, but, again, it may take up to 24 hours to disable the setting.

Security features are only as strong as their weakest links. In the case of iOS 27's Impersonation Risk Detection, there are two main weak links. First, this feature is disabled by default. Most people aren't going to dig deep enough into settings to discover it accidentally, and the feature isn't going to be used widely unless people know about it. Second, this feature also depends on app developers adding support for it. Big tech companies and indie developers may adopt it reasonably quickly, but other developers may not rush to implement this feature.

There's also the fact that plenty of apps have already spent a lot of resources building up their own security infrastructure, and they may not necessarily see value in adding support for this feature. Here in India, all banking and payment apps show multiple full-screen warnings when you try to make a payment while on a phone call. Some apps may even disable payment features if they detect that a screen-sharing app is installed on your device. So, really, it will come down to how app developers respond to this feature.

Apple says that Impersonation Risk Detection performs its analysis on-device, and that the data used to generate the risk level doesn't leave your device. The company also highlights that the contents of your email, photos, or messages are not analyzed for the risk assessment. When an app requests a risk assessment, Apple claims it only receives information about the type of action you performed in that specific app. Once the risk level is generated, apps don't receive any additional data about you.

title: The iPhone X Literally Changed How We Use Our Devices
description: Those touch gestures took some getting used to back in 2017.
fullText:
Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET, and Popular Science.

That was the year Apple released the iPhone X, introducing the device's most radical change since its first iteration. (Perhaps only to be surpassed this year by the iPhone Duo.) It's funny to think about it today, but back in 2017, the iPhone X's single pane of glass was disruptive, to say the least. Where was the Home button? Without it, how could you do anything? That confusion inspired Lifehacker to publish "The iPhone X Gestures You Should Master," a guide to navigating your newly designed iPhone.

We had to learn to swipe up from the bottom of the display to go home; to swipe along the bottom to switch from app to app; to swipe down from the top right to access Control Center; to swipe down from the top left to access Notification Center. We even had to relearn reachability: Instead of lightly double-tapping the Home button to bring the screen down, you had to swipe down on the bottom of the display.

Reviewing these things now, it all seems so obvious, even second nature. Nearly another decade has passed since we published that story, and by now, most iOS users are accostumed to a Home button-free life. But looking through the comments on this nearly decade-old piece, it's clear the transition was anything but smooth. One user complained about how smartphone gestures were making everything more confusing. Another bemoaned how switching between their iPhone and iPad meant jumping between two different gesture systems. Fast forward to 2026, and it's near impossible to imagine going back.

Apple didn't immediately stop making iPhones with Home buttons—it also released the iPhone 8 and 8 Plus the same year as the iPhone X—but the writing was on the wall. Soon after, only the SE line shipped with the old design, and even iPads adopted an edge-to-edge display.

With the launch of the iPhone 16e in 2025, Apple officially retired the once-essential Home button. Though you can still buy and use second-hand devices that have one (the 2022 iPhone SE can even run iOS 27), it's clear the company has moved on, and the gestures once so foreign they once prompted us to publish a guide to their use are now as innate as doing things the old way. Perhaps in another 10 years, wearables and hand gestures will have changed everything again, and we'll look back with nostalgia on an era when we had to touch our devices at all.

fullText:
Big screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closed

Google’s latest folding phone sticks with its tried and tested design of a traditional phone shape when closed and almost square when open, in the face of new competition from Apple’s squat iPhone fold.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is Google’s fourth-generation folder and is still one of the only models with a full water and dust resistance rating similar to standard slab phones. It costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799), which is £50 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year as the pressure of RAMageddon continues to push up prices.

The 11 Pro Fold looks identical to previous models, but it is 19g lighter and fractionally slimmer in all directions with a slightly larger outside screen. Unlike Samsung’s slender Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra or squat models such as Apple’s iPhone Duo or the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the Pixel has the same ratio screen as Google’s slab phones and so handles precisely like them when shut with a bright and smooth 6.5in display.

Opened up, the internal screen is essentially square, which allows you to run two full-size apps side by side but is less ideal for video. The display is very bright, crisp and smooth, but the crease where it folds is more visible and detectable with your fingers than the best rivals. Like all foldable phones the screen is also delicate compared with standard hardened glass phones.

The back of the phone hides the excellent Qi2 magnetic charging and accessory support from last year, while Google’s gimmicky HiLight notification LED, as seen on the other Pro Pixels, replaces the camera’s flash.

Outside screen: 6.5in FHD+ 120Hz OLED (399ppi)

Inside screen: 8in 120Hz OLED (372ppi)

Camera: 48MP wide, 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP 5x telephoto; two 10MP selfie cameras

Connectivity: 5G, eSim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, Thread, GNSS

Water resistance: IP68 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)

Dimensions folded: 155.2 x 76 x 10.1mm

Dimensions unfolded: 155.2 x 150.4 x 5mm

The 11 Pro Fold has the same Tensor G6 chip from the other Pixel 11 models with 16GB of memory, which works very well for all kinds of multitasking, remaining snappy and responsive with multiple apps on screen. It handles light gaming, but can’t match rivals for raw performance.

The battery life is a little shorter than last year’s model and rivals, lasting about 36 hours between charges when used on a mix of 5G and wifi with the screens in active use for about 2.5 hours each for browsing, messaging, apps and photos. Most will have to charge it nightly, but even on the heaviest of use days the Pixel managed to end the day without requiring a top-up.

The Fold runs the latest version of Android 17 with all of Google’s AI tools, including Gemini’s proactive system, the new supercharged voice dictation feature and six months of Google AI Pro subscription.

Many of Google’s more creative AI tools, including the Omni video creation tool, Circle to Search and Gemini’s information cards benefit from the larger internal screen. Google has made a number of modifications to Android to better fit the folding form, including a floating taskbar and a split-screen mode that can resize apps beyond the bounds of the physical display introduced last year.

The bubbles system, which was primarily used for messaging apps, has been revamped to allow as many as five apps of any kind to be opened as floating windows on top of a single or split-screen apps and minimised to a little taskbar. But it isn’t as flexible as Samsung’s true desktop-like floating window system that can be resized and placed anywhere on the screen.

The 11 Pro Fold will be supported until August 2033 with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest supported devices available.

The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google and third-party shops, and self-repair with manuals and parts is due to be available.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold contains 24% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free.

The Pixel Fold has some of the best cameras on a foldable phone, including three on the back and two very good selfie cameras, one in each screen.

The rear cameras include a new 48MP main camera with a larger sensor, matching that in the regular Pixel 11, which captures better detail and has significantly better lowlight performance than its predecessor. The 10.5MP ultrawide camera is the same as last year and is still as solid this year. The 10.8MP 5x telephoto is also the same and shoots good photos that meaningfully reduce the distance to objects. It has a solid digital zoom that stretches up to 30x magnification, but not the generative AI zoom of the Pixel 11 Pro.

The Fold also has the new software features from the other Pixel 11 phones, including Camera Looks, which allows you to customise the processing of your photos for different styles. Magic Capture shoots video and photos automatically with one button, while the Creator suite helps you storyboard, trim and produce video content for social media.

The camera also has tricks to make use of the folding form, including modes to shoot when propped up and the excellent Made You Look feature that displays an animated character that reacts to your kid’s smiling to help take better photos.

Overall, the 11 Pro Fold has an excellent set of cameras that don’t feel a significant downgrade on top regular smartphones.

The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799).

For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs £879, Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079, the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs £1,899, the iPhone Duo costs £1,999 and the Honor Magic V6 costs £1,499.99.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a fairly minor hardware update for Google’s folding phone line, which makes it slightly lighter, smaller, brighter and faster, while keeping its overall look and feel the same.

It has great AI tools, slick software and some of the very best cameras. The inside screen is super bright and crisp, but the crease down the middle is more noticeable than rivals, the battery life is a bit short and it is thick and heavy compared to the best from rival Samsung.

As with all foldables the inside screen can be permanently marked by a fingernail if you press hard enough, so you must still be careful with it compared with a standard Pixel.

But if you want a folding phone to be exactly the same as a regular one when closed, the Pixel Fold is the one to get.

Pros: just like a regular Pixel when closed, good tablet screen, dust and water resistant, Qi2 magnetic accessory and charging, good performance, great cameras with 5x zoom, great software packed with cutting-edge AI, six months of Google AI Pro included, seven years of software updates.

Cons: very expensive, more fragile and costlier to repair than a regular Pixel, thick and heavy, cameras can’t match regular Pixel 11 Pro, battery life could be better.

fullText:
Criminals exploit demand for iPhone 18 Pro and foldable Duo to trick people eager to get their hands on one

Apple has just launched a range of new iPhones, including a foldable handset, just as you decide it is time to replace your own ageing mobile. But you balk at the £1,199 price tag for the cheapest of the new options.

Searching online for a better price with the words “cheap”, “iPhone” and “deal”, you come across a website which offers an iPhone 18 Pro for a couple of hundred pounds less than the Apple site. You pay for the new phone via a bank transfer and wait for it to arrive.

But the website is a fraud - one of hundreds set up in the days before the new Apple phones were announced – and is designed to scam money out of people eager to get their hands on one of the new handsets.

Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone, on Wednesday, as well as two new iPhone 18 Pro models.

At the same time, criminals were building up networks of fake sites. Security researchers found a large spike in the number of scam sites registered with “Apple” and “iPhone”, among other keywords, in their domain names.

It is expected that the number will proliferate into the hundreds.

Alexandre François, who investigates scams for the intelligence company WhoisXML API, says the days before and after the announcement of the phones typically see a glut of domain names being registered by criminals. Some are then developed into phishing sites in order to dupe people.

“Some are flagged as dangerous by dozens of security engines, yet they are still absent from the blocklists that browsers and security tools rely on, so for most people nothing stops the page from loading,” he says.

“In each of the last four iPhone launches, domain registrations referencing the new model peaked on ‘keynote day’ – the launch day itself: more than 200 new domains within 24 hours, against zero or one on a normal day.”

The domain names will often include words such as “Apple” and “iPhone 18”. The content of a developed site will look convincingly realistic as fraudsters frequently use AI to mimic genuine retailers.

One site found by François, an iPhone Pro Max, in three different colours, was advertised with claims of an “all-day battery”.

The release of technical specifications following the launch allows fraudsters to build more convincing websites. François says it then “becomes much easier to convince people that what they are looking at is a real iPhone”.

The sites may also claim to offer early access to the devices, as well as cheaper prices. The new iPhone 18 Pro starts at £1,199 officially, while the 18 Pro Max at £1,299, so expect the scam sites to quote prices substantially lower.

As with many scams, fraudsters may give people a deadline to buy – such as a few hours – to encourage them to abandon caution in a bid to land a bargain.

The sites will often only take payment via bank transfer to avoid giving people the protections available when you pay with a debit and credit card.

Remember what is on sale. So far, the iPhone Duo and the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have been announced – but not the standard iPhone 18. Pages which claim to be selling it now or taking deposits are fakes.

François says Apple does not operate lotteries and does not recruit people to test phones.

Legitimate websites will offer consumers a variety of ways to pay – debit and credit cards among them. Some fraudulent sites will insist payment is made using cryptocurrency, which should act as an immediate red flag.

Apple says its Safari browser has a warning for fraudulent websites that alerts users to phishing or malware sites.

If you find you have given out your financial details, contact your bank and Report Fraud. And then change your passwords.

title: How the iPhone Duo Stacks Up to the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8
description: How does Apple's new foldable compare to the rest?
fullText:
After years of rumors, Apple finally made a foldable: the iPhone Duo. The initial reaction online has been mostly positive—particularly how iOS adapts to the phone and that cool transition wallpaper effect—but it begs the question: How does Apple's new device compare to the folding phones already on the market?

The iPhone Duo is now competing against the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which I'll focus on here rather than the Z Fold 8 Ultra). There are key similarities and differences between the three handsets that suggest whether or not the iPhone Duo will be a success. And having used both Google and Samsung foldables in the past, I have some ideas about what the iPhone Duo needs to get right.

Google and Samsung have been doing this longer than Apple has, and their phones are thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo. That might make a difference once Apple's handset gets out into the world, with preorders set to start on Friday, Oct. 16. You can also see here that Apple and Samsung have gone for the "passport" style approach: Displays that are shorter and wider, which means a more tablet-style main display. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold has the aspect ratio of a standard smartphone when closed, with a main display that's more square.

You can see how the passport-style foldable compares to the more traditional foldable form factor in the display dimensions too: There's a lot more vertical space on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold when all of these foldables are closed shut, which is quite a consideration. If you're like me, you'll end up using your foldable closed more often than unfolded, in which case the outer display becomes very important. (But more on that later.) It's worth knowing that both Apple and Google rely on Samsung to supply their phone displays, as per industry sources.

If you'd like a foldable phone, it's going to cost you, whichever brand you favor. The iPhone Duo starts a little higher than the competition and goes up to 2TB of storage—something Google and Samsung don't do. It's worth mentioning RAM here too: The iPhone Duo has 12GB, the Google phone comes with 16GB, and Samsung offers either 12GB or 16GB in the Galaxy Z Fold 8, depending on the amount of storage you buy. But it's not an even comparison: The Duo runs iOS, which has different RAM requirements than Android devices.

Cameras abound on foldable phones—you need a selfie camera for the inner display and the outer display—and it's notable that Apple isn't telling anyone the specs of its inner selfie cameras. Google's foldable is the only one with a telephoto camera. In the modern era, software processing is just as important as hardware specs, so how the handsets compare on this front is to some extent subjective. It'll be interesting to see how photos from the iPhone Duo stand up against those on the iPhone 18 Pro, which has a more advanced camera system.

The iPhone Duo doesn't have face unlock as the Google and Samsung phones do, and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 doesn't have the IP68 waterproofing of the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold (though this doesn't last). Battery life is a key consideration when picking a smartphone, but the capacity numbers here can only tell us so much. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 4,806 mAh battery, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has a 4,800 mAh battery, and Apple isn't revealing the battery capacity on the iPhone Duo—though it does say you can get up to 44 hours of video playback between charges on the outer display. Software optimization and other factors play a role too, so some real-world testing will be needed for a proper comparison.

Speaking of software, there's the iOS and Android divide, of course. From what we've seen of iOS on the iPhone Duo, it looks like an elegant and thoughtful adaptation, with shifting buttons, split keyboards, a dual pane mode, and some other nice touches—no doubt helped by Apple's iPad experience. To my eye, it seems like a more fluid experience than what you get on an Android foldable, though that's not to say you get a bad experience on Google and Samsung phones.

Spec sheets can only get you so far, and while the iPhone Duo has made a bold impression based on what we've seen from Apple so far, no one has properly used one yet. The true test for whether the foldable iPhone is a hit or not is going to depend on how well it works through all the moments of day-to-day life.

I've spent several years using foldable phones from Samsung and Google, and aside from the rather prohibitive cost, the main issue that makes me still prefer standard phone form factors is that, for most of the time, there's no reason to open up the full display—which means you're left with a device that's chunky and heavy, with no real upside. Checking messages on the go, making contactless payments, taking photos: the majority of phone tasks don't need or suit a tablet-sized screen. That's what all of these foldables are fighting against. Would you use an iPad to take a photo at a gig, call your parents, or find your way around in an unfamiliar city?

Apple seems to have the software experience right, and the iPhone Duo looks as well crafted as you would expect a foldable iPhone to be—but even if you can foot the bill for one of these, you might find that the cost of using a thicker, heavier, smaller phone isn't worth it, just so you can occasionally have a bigger screen available. The iPhone Duo actually stacks up pretty well against the foldables from Samsung and Google, but its real competition is going to come from other iPhones.

title: Six Ways the iPhone Duo Has an Edge Over Android Foldables
description: Though late to the party, Apple's first foldable brings a lot of innovative design to the table.
fullText:
I've followed the foldable smartphone space for seven years now, but I’ve still never wanted to buy one. But the iPhone Duo is making me doubt my convictions, and not just because I’m an iPhone user. Until now, foldable smartphones felt like a work in progress to me, requiring a sacrifice or two (or three) with either the hardware or the software.

But with the launch of the iPhone Duo, it feels like this everything is finally coming together. Apple's hardware and the software appear to be working hand in hand to provide a seamless, and even fun, foldable experience. It still feels like choosing the Duo instead carries its own share of compromises—missing Face ID, no telephoto lens, and the lack of an Action button)—but what the new device brings to the table might make up for all of that.

It’s a trick, but it’s surprising no one thought of this before. When you open the iPhone Duo, the cover screen performs a blurred animation that seamlessly continues to the inner screen. What’s on the cover screen appears on the right side of the inner screen. The interface also adapts to the hinge and the degree of folding. Make it a tent, and it shows the Stand By widgets. When watching media, you can prop it up like a laptop, and the interface splits in two as well, with the top half showing the media, and controls on the bottom half (assuming the app has been optimized to do so, anyway). If you’re playing a game or watching a movie on the inner screen, closing the Duo will switch the content to the cover screen, with the animation, and without skipping a beat. This is the kind of seamless device/software integration that's tough for Android devices to compete with.

Apple is late to the foldable party, but at least it has caught up in the screen and hinge tech. Of course, we won’t know exactly how creaseless it is until we can all get our hands on the iPhone Duo, but based on the coverage so far, it is at least fairly creaseless. In day-to-day use, you might not even notice it.

More interesting is the inner display tech: Apple is bringing a version of the nano-texture display from the MacBook Pro line to this device. The matte display fights reflections, but it also hides the crease—something that’s harder to do with the glossy panels sported by Android foldables.

As noted, the real hardware-software advantage shows up in how iOS works. Because of the shorter display, Apple has chosen to dedicate the right-hand side edge to the Dock and toolbar controls, an interesting choice in terms of reachability and design.

The usable space isn’t compromised, either with the cover screen or the inner display. Adapting and moving the toolbar, and bringing third-party apps along for the ride, is no easy feat. It’s also something that would be extremely difficult to pull off on the Android side: It would require a design directive from Google, and manufacturers would have to find their own ways to implement it.

It will be interesting to see how third-party developers adapt to the new screen and layout options. Apple already showcased how media apps like Netflix are taking advantage of the split-screen interface design. Zoom’s example, where the screen sharing is on one side and the meeting participants are on the other, is quite smart, too.

How you end up using the inner screen on a foldable is all down to how developers take advantage of it. Sure, you can put two apps side by side, but how often are people really going to do that? But the fact that you have an iPad mini-sized canvas, along with upcoming support for the Apple Pencil, sets the stage for creative uses of the expanding display. Conversely, Samsungdropped support for its stylus from the Fold series last year.

Under-display selfie cameras are not new—Samsung tried it in Fold 3, and gave up in the Fold 7. The under-display camera just wasn’t as good. This is the first time that Apple is trying it, and we will have to test it out before we can make a judgment on how well it performs.

But that's not the only camera-related feature in the iPhone Duo. While it's missing a telephoto lens, the way Apple is using the second screen in the camera and FaceTime is very interesting. When you're photographing someone with the Duo unfolded, the cover screen becomes a live preview, so the subjects can see themselves, and guide you as well. To make it easier to capture moments with kids, the outer camera can show fun Snoopy graphics. Even FaceTime has a Duo mode where a participant can be shown on the cover screen.

Most foldable smartphones lose out when it comes to dust and water resistance. The design itself means you have to be careful with dust, especially around the hinges. The Samsung Fold 8, for example, has an IP48 rating. The iPhone Duo gets the full IP68 sealing treatment. An IP68 rating means that the iPhone Duo is fully dust-protected, and it can survive under shallow 1.5 meter deep water for 30 minutes. The Samsung Galaxy Fold 8 lacks a dust-sealing rating, though it does offer stronger water resistance.

All that new tech does come at a cost. The first is literal: the $1,999 starting price, or more than buying an iPhone and an iPad mini combined. The foldable design ushers in a new era of iPhone innovation, but it’s also leaving behind features that iPhone users have come to love and expect. There’s no Face ID, no Action button, no real optical zoom, and no physical SIM card slot, all lacking in a device that’s quite heavy (254 g) compared to the iPhone 18 Pro (211 grams). Ultimately, the market (and buyers' wallets) will decide if these tradeoffs are worth it, but if you ask me, the Duo makes the most compelling case for a foldable yet. 

iPhone Duo pre-orders open October 16, and the device won’t ship until October 23.

title: 12 of the Best iPhone 18 Pro Features That Are Missing From the Foldable Duo
description: The iPhone Duo lacks quite a few useful camera features.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo is both the most exciting (and expensive) product from Apple's September hardware event. The Duo is Apple's first foldable, equipped with new features not present in the company's other iPhones. On the flip side, designing a foldable smartphone comes with a bunch of compromises, which means that the iPhone Duo misses out on a lot of features when compared with the iPhone 18 Pro and the 18 Pro Max. Yes, even if you pay $1,999 (going all the way up to $3,199 for the 2TB variant) for an iPhone Duo, you won't be getting all the best new iPhone features this year. Here's every feature that the iPhone Duo misses out on.

Unlike the iPhone 18 Pro series (or any iPhone since the 15), the foldable iPhone doesn't get a programmable Action button. It doesn't even have a mute switch, which means that its only buttons are for volume control and power. The Action button can be mapped to simple tasks such as taking screenshots, or more complex automations of your choice, and it'll be missed on the foldable iPhone.

The iPhone Duo ships with a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera on the outer display, which is a lower-resolution sensor than the one on the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. The two 18 Pro series phones ship with an 18-megapixel Center Stage camera for selfies. The iPhone Duo also has an under-display front camera, and since Apple hasn't disclosed its megapixel count, it's safe to say it's also less than the 18 Pros. However, by its nature, the Duo has an interesting advantage here: If you're taking selfies with the device unfolded, you get to use the far superior "rear" camera sensor, as the front display becomes your viewfinder. Anyone using the Duo for selfies this way will shoot better pictures than those using the front camera on an iPhone 18 Pro.

Variable aperture is one of the best new camera features of the iPhone 18 Pro series. The primary rear camera lets you control aperture, which opens up the possibility for better quality photos, enhanced depth of field effects, and more creative control over your photography. Unfortunately, the iPhone Duo misses out on this feature.

Apple also announced a new standard to combat AI-morphed images. Apple Reference Image allows you to verify that an image was captured using an iPhone 18 Pro device, and that it wasn't generated by AI. For some reason, however, this feature isn't coming to the iPhone Duo.

Apple decided to go with two rear cameras in the iPhone Duo, which means that the telephoto lens gets a miss. The iPhone 18 Pro series has 4x and 8x optical zoom options, both of which won't be available on the iPhone Duo. You'll be limited to a zoom range of 0.5x to 2x on the foldable iPhone, across both the ultrawide and Fusion cameras.

Spatial photos, Spatial videos, and ProRAW are all features targeted at professional photographers and videographers. These features are available in the iPhone 18 Pro series, but not on the iPhone Duo.

Apple included a "studio-quality" four-mic array in the iPhone 18 Pro and the 18 Pro Max. The aim is to enhance audio quality when you're shooting video. The iPhone Duo misses out on this feature too.

Apple chose to give the iPhone Duo Touch ID, which means that you can use your fingerprint to unlock the device. While the lack of Face ID may initially seem like a big miss, I think it makes perfect sense for a device that has multiple "front" cameras. Rather than placing the Face ID sensor near every camera, Apple opted for the more practical alternative. Plus, you can unlock your iPhone Duo with your Apple Watch, if you have one.

LiDAR sensors measure distances between two objects, creating 3D scans of objects in the real world, and even mapping the layout of your home for 3D models. Your iPhone ships with an app called Measure, which works well with Pro series iPhones because those devices have a LiDAR scanner. The iPhone Duo misses out.

This year, Apple reserved all the fun iPhone colors for the 18 Pro and the 18 Pro Max, including the new Glacier and Burgundy color variants. I wish Apple had added at least one of those to the iPhone Duo, as the foldable iPhone is only available in "Night Sky" (dark blue) or white.

The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone to ship with two eSIM slots globally. The iPhone 18 Pro devices will be eSIM-exclusive in 12 countries, but not in the rest of the world. The 18 Pro will ship with at least one physical SIM slot in most regions. An eSIM is great for those who never swap SIM cards or travel often, but having the option of a physical SIM is also useful. It allows you to use cheap prepaid travel SIMs when abroad, and offers you the flexibility to keep swapping SIMs quickly.

title: Here's Why You Should Care About the iPhone 18 Pro's 'Vapor Chambers'
description: The iPhone 18 Pro's vapor chamber is three times larger than the previous generation. What does that even mean?
fullText:
During Apple’s big hardware announcement on Wednesday, the company placed a particular emphasis on the vapor chamber in the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The glossed-over explanation is that these new vapor chambers can improve performance and reduce heat generation. But how exactly? And what does that mean for the phones you’re planning to buy?

On a very simple level, vapor chambers work similarly to liquid cooling in other electronics systems like some desktop PCs or server racks. The goal is to carry heat away from the processor to keep it cool, so it can do more work without overheating. A cooler processor is a more efficient processor, which means it runs better.

Except, unlike a PC or server rack, a phone is a tight, compact system. There’s not enough space to heat water and then pump it away to a different location to cool it down. Instead, a vapor chamber is a thin, hollow chamber, typically made of either copper or stainless steel, with a small amount of liquid inside. When the liquid inside heats up, it becomes a gas, which then expands outwards, dispersing the heat throughout the body of your phone, rather than keeping it all close to the processor. As it gets further away from the source of heat, the vapor cools back down and becomes a liquid again.

Since the chamber is sealed, the liquid can’t evaporate and escape, meaning that the fluid can theoretically keep cycling through the chamber indefinitely for the life of the phone. Most manufacturers also pair this with some form of heat sink, like thin sheets of graphite or copper. Or, in the case of the new iPhone 18 Pro, both.

Keeping your phone cool is a massive problem compared to other electronic devices you might have, simply because they’re so small, yet so powerful. A moderately powered laptop like a MacBook Air can get away with a combination of conductive heat sinks, a metal frame, and low heat-generating processors to stay functional, while high-powered gaming laptops have space to stuff in large, laborious fans.

Your phone, however, needs to fit in your pocket, and a huge chunk of the space inside needs to be devoted to the battery to make sure it lasts long enough to get through the day. Once you account for all the processors, sensors, and antennas that a phone needs, there’s scarcely any space left for heat dissipation. That’s a huge part of why phones generally don’t have as powerful processors as tablets or laptops. Physically, it’s not impossible to fit a high-powered chip in a pocketable device. But it would likely generate so much heat that it would destroy itself without proper heat dissipation, which would make your phone too big for a pocket.

This kind of heat dissipation matters even more if you happen to live in places with warm climates. For example, I live in Texas. Even when driving inside an air-conditioned car, if my phone is in the sunlight, it can start to overheat. When I previously had a Pixel 6 Pro, it would occasionally shut off (taking my navigation with it) simply because it wasn’t in the shade. After upgrading to a Pixel 9 Pro, which does have a vapor chamber, I never noticed this problem—though this is obviously anecdotal.

Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro’s vapor chamber has three times the surface area of the previous generation, which theoretically should mean better cooling and, thus, better performance. But does that mean you need to decide what phone to buy based on how big a phone’s vapor chamber is, or whether it has one at all?

Well, yes and no. It turns out that outside the Apple ecosystem, Android phones have been using vapor chambers for years, and you might not have even noticed. The existence of vapor chambers is increasingly becoming standard, so unless you have an old phone that frequently overheats, or you’re looking to buy a phone a few generations behind, you probably don’t need to go out of your way to make sure your phone has one.

And whether bigger is necessarily better is also a bit of a gray area. All other things being equal, yes, a larger vapor chamber will dissipate heat better and keep your phone cooler. But all other things are rarely equal. A larger vapor chamber also means the manufacturer can put a more powerful processor inside and achieve the same thermal balance. So, a phone could theoretically be equally likely to overheat, but do more before it does.

Figuring out the right balance between processing power and heat dissipation is the kind of thing best left to the engineers and dedicated hobbyists. But there are a couple of things the average person can take away from this. First, if you live in a warm climate, better heat dissipation is always going to be better. Your phone isn’t running at full power all day, but the Texas sun is. So, if you’re worried about your environment causing overheating problems, check phone reviews for how well it handles heat. More importantly, consider the power needs you have for your device before you buy. If you just use your phone to scroll TikTok and reply to emails, you probably don’t need an overpowered processor, but if you plan to edit 4K videos or play graphically intense mobile games, then better thermal regulation could do you some good.

title: Will the iPad Ever Be a Worthy Mac Replacement?
description: iOS 9 brought us multitasking on iPad. Here's how far we've come since.
fullText:
Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET and Popular Science.

For the first five years of its life, the iPad could only run one app at a time. Then, iOS 9 changed everything. That update, released 10 years ago this month, introduced multitasking to the Apple tablet for the first time. "Split View" let you run two apps side-by-side at once; "Slide Over" gave you quick access to a third app in an iPhone-style window; and Picture in Picture made it possible to watch a video while working on something else. In an article published at the time, these changes prompted Lifehacker to proclaim that "iOS 9 actually makes the iPad usable for work."

In total, you could have up to four different windows on screen through this concoction of features, a huge improvement over the previous limit of "one." Coupled with the new keyboard shortcuts, iOS 9 transformed the iPad, and brought it closer to the laptop replacement so many users wanted it to be. "Closer" being the key word there.

While iOS 9 made it possible to focus on more than one app at a time, it didn't address other iPad limitations that made it difficult for computer users to fully make the switch. In the 11 years since that update, Apple has chipped away at those issues slowly but surely, while upgrading the iPad's hardware exponentially. In iOS 11, Apple made it easier to launch an app into Split View from the Dock, and introduced cross-app drag and drop. With iPadOS 13, Apple introduced a desktop-class version of Safari, and rolled out the Files app, which even supported hard drives and SD cards. iPadOS 15 improved Split View and Slide Over accessibility, and made it possible to multitask with multiple windows from one app.

We're at the point where, on the surface, the iPad can be considered Apple's answer to the touchscreen computer, especially when paired with a keyboard and trackpad. But in practical use, it's evident the iPad still isn't a Mac, even in cases where the iPad supports the apps and utilities you use on Mac. iPadOS doesn't feel designed for computer tasks; it feels like computer tasks were retrofitted to iPadOS. That doesn't mean things like multitasking and file support aren't welcome features, but the experience isn't as refined as it is on macOS. What's more, there is evidence Apple agrees the two devices are just too different, as rumors suggest the company might release a touchscreen MacBook as soon as next year.

For me, iPadOS still feels at its best when I use one app at a time. All the above efforts to change its nature aside, that's probably because the iPad was originally designed that way.

title: Apple Just Announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max
description: Apple's latest "Pro" iPhones are official.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo will inevitably steal tech headlines this week. After all, Apple finally made a foldable iPhone to compete with options from Samsung and Google. But while an iPhone with two displays is novel and exciting, it's also going to be expensive. I imagine there are many in the market for a new iPhone who aren't interested in spending as much as $2,000. There are also likely customers who don't want a foldable iPhone, and would prefer the standard smartphone design they're used to. That's where the iPhone 18 Pro comes in.

If you have an iPhone 17 Pro, you might confuse it for the iPhone 18 Pro. Indeed, Apple hasn't changed the overall design much this year, which is to be expected. The iPhone 17 Pro refreshed the Pro iPhone design with its large camera bump and plane of glass for MagSafe charging. The 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max aren't much different—though now the metal is color-matched to the back glass.

That being said, there are some changes here you may notice upon closer examination. Perhaps first you'd notice the 18 Pro's Dynamic Island is smaller than it has been on previous Pro iPhones. With it, you're able to run three tasks at once, rather than two. That may prove useful depending on what you're doing, or it may end up cluttering the top of your iPhone. 18 Pro users will have to be the judge. You'd also notice some new color options not available on the iPhone 17 Pro, which I'll cover below.

The displays will remain the same sizes as last year—6.3 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro, and 6.9 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. But now, these displays use a more efficient LPTO+ technology.

Like the iPhone Duo, the iPhone 18 Pros come with Apple's new A20 Pro chip built on 2nm technology. The company touts how the new chip is great for processing AI on-device, with a six-core CPU, seven-core GPU, new Neural Accelerators, and a second Neural Engine. Apple focused on the A20 Pro's thermal cooling with the new vapor chamber in the 18 Pro. Apple says this means there are significant sustained performance improvements over the iPhone 17 Pro.

Apple says this chip has the fastest CPU in a smartphone, with 50% better memory bandwidth. But, as with all performance claims, we'll have to wait until testers try out the A20 Pro for themselves. Still, Apple's newest chips always improve on the previous generation by some degree, so it's safe to say the 18 Pro (and the Duo at that) will be the fastest iPhones yet.

Apple also says the iPhone 18 Pro has 36 hours of battery life while streaming video, while iPhone 18 Pro Max has 45 hours. The company says five minutes of charging gets you six hours of video playback.

Perhaps the biggest change for the iPhone 18 Pro this year is its cameras. Apple's Pro iPhones are known for their shooters, but for the 18 Pros, Apple has taken things up a notch. For the first time, these iPhones have variable apertures. When using the 48MP main camera, your iPhone can physically open and close its aperture to control how much light hits the sensor—up to 50% more light than before. That offers two benefits: In dim environments, you can let in more light than you normally could. You can also use the aperture to control the depth of field, or the background blur. A large aperture (more light) means a blurrier background, while a smaller aperture (less light) means a cleaner background.

Apple also introduced Pro Controls, which has been sorely missing on the iPhone. You now can control white balance and shutter speed, and check the histogram. This mode works for both photography and videography. There's now a new "smart focus tracking" feature that uses AI to keep focus on a subject. Photographic Styles get some additional upgrades and controls, and Time-Lapse also supports 4K. With the 18 Pro, Apple is rolling out a "reference" feature to ensure that an original shot can be confirmed if an edit is later made with AI. Apple calls this a "digital negative."

As previously mentioned, the iPhone 18 Pro's colors may be one of the most recognisably "new" features of this generation. Apple is rolling out color options in "Burgundy," "Glacier," and Silver, though the first two may be the more distinct of the bunch. Still, it's more variation than we have on the Duo.

Everything is getting more expensive, thanks to RAMaggedon, and the iPhone 18 Pro is no exception. Apple is raising the starting price this year to $1,199 for the 256GB model, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for the 256GB variant.

Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro will be available to preorder on Saturday, Sept. 12 at 12 a.m. PT (3 a.m. ET). The devices then go on sale Friday, Sept. 18.

title: Where’s the iPhone 18?
description: Apple is giving its iPhone release schedule the biggest shake-up in history.
fullText:
There was something different about today's "Surprise and Shine" launch event from Apple: We didn't get the unveiling of the iPhone 18.

For the first time since Apple started releasing multiple iPhones per year, which was 2013 with the arrival of the iPhone 5c and the iPhone 5s (simpler times), we have several pro-level handsets without the standard version to accompany them. So what's behind the shift? And is the iPhone 18 canceled? Apple, predictably, isn't saying, but we've got enough clues to make an informed guess.

If you've been keeping up with Apple rumors since the launch of the iPhone 17, you'll know that this has long been predicted—notably by the most respected purveyor of Apple leaks in the business, reporter Mark Gurman. Gurman was predicting in Bloomberg as far back as November 2025 that we would only get the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the folding iPhone Duo in 2026.

The reason? According to Gurman, it's to spread out revenue more evenly across the year, rather than having most of the iPhones unveiled every September. It also takes some of the pressure off Apple's marketing teams and reduces the likelihood of mishaps like that Siri AI upgrade—which was announced way before it was ready. Gurman also went on record as saying that this is likely to be the norm for "years to come," so get used to it.

However, Gurman wasn't the first to break the news. In May of 2025, Wayne Ma at The Information reported that Apple would hold the standard iPhone 18 model over until 2027, based on conversations with anonymous supply chain sources. As per that report, one of the motivations behind the shift was to make more space for the folding iPhone, which makes sense considering it's Apple's first attempt at the form factor.

Just a day later, well-known and usually well-informed Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo backed up the story, saying that we'd see the foldable iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the iPhone Air 2 (then called the iPhone 18 Slim) in September 2026. Apart from that last handset, he was right.

Kuo added an extra reason for the shift as well: Competition from phone manufacturers based in Asia. A lot of these manufacturers release their flagship handsets during the first half of the year, including Samsung, and as far as Apple is concerned, that can leave it playing catch-up by the time September rolls around.

While the iPhone 18 was a no-show at the "Surprise and Shine" event, there's no indication that it's been canceled. Apple still wants to cater to those who'd rather spend a little less on their iPhones (the iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,119), and the most educated guesses we've seen suggest we'll get the base version of the phone sometime in March.

It's unlikely to be on its own either. We're also expecting to see the iPhone 18e and the iPhone Air 2 appear at the same time, following on from the iPhone 17e (launched in March 2026) and the original iPhone Air (launched in September 2025, alongside the iPhone 17 series).

And that "e" phone series set the foundation for the calendar shift we've now seen with the standard iPhone 18 model. The first of these more affordable handsets, the iPhone SE, showed up in March 2016—it was then followed by the iPhone SE 2 (April 2020), the iPhone SE 3 (March 2022), and the iPhone 16e (February 2025). That shows Apple has been eyeing up the February-March-April slot for non-pro-level iPhones for a decade at this point.

The rumors so far suggest the iPhone 18 will use an A20 chipset, while we're likely to get a RAM bump as well. We now know that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have a smaller Dynamic Island, with the ability to show up to three Live Activities, and that's something that should carry across to the standard model (along with iOS 27).

Apple didn't mention the iPhone 18 at all today—not even in a post-credits sequence—but it would be a major surprise if the handset didn't make a belated appearance sometime in the first quarter of next year. If this is the iPhone that's for you, you're just going to have to wait a little while longer.

title: The iPhone 18 Pro Series Comes With Big Gains in Battery Life
