fullText:
While the iPhone 18 Pro looks similar to last year's model, the internals are a different story. The new A20 Pro processor with 32 Neural Engine cores will go a long way helping with on-device AI tasks—but you might not feel those differences all the time.

The new updates to battery life and charging, however, will make an actual difference in daily use on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Apple is promising the best battery life on an iPhone yet, and is finally supporting faster wired charging.

According to Apple, the regular sized iPhone 18 Pro will have the same battery life as the outgoing, larger iPhone 17 Pro Max model, which is quite a big deal. Apple is combining the efficiency gains in the A20 Pro chip with new battery technology to deliver this large leap in battery life.

You will get 45 hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and 36 hours on the iPhone 18 Pro model. The iPhone 18 Pro will last 24 hours per charge, while the 18 Pro Max can go up to 30 hours.

According to Apple, this is based on tests performed with Apple's 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with a 60W max charging speed. Wired fast charging is also supported with 60W-capable USB-C cables and USB PD 3.1 adapters that support Adjustable Voltage Supply.

The world of Android flagships is filled with quick-charging smartphones, and some of that clout will now come over to the iPhone as well. title: Apple Just Announced the Foldable 'iPhone Duo'
description: It's Apple's first foldable smartphone.
fullText:
Since Apple announced the date of its big September event, we've expected the company to reveal the "iPhone Ultra," its first foldable smartphone. As it turns out, half of that prediction came true: While the company did indeed showcase the first iPhone to transform from smartphone to tablet, it isn't actually called the Ultra. Instead, the company surprised us all with a new name: iPhone Duo.

It's immediately apparent that the iPhone Duo has a much different design than any iPhone Apple has ever made. This device is foldable, which means it has two functioning displays, depending on how you use it. When closed, the Duo has a funkier 5.4-inch display than the one you might be used to on an iPhone, but it's fully functional. You don't actually have to open up the Duo to use it: You can text, browse Safari, play games, and do whatever you normally would on your iPhone from here. The selfie cam and two rear cameras mean you can take FaceTime calls and shoot photos and videos while the Duo is in this position. If you never wanted to open up your Duo, you would probably never have to.

Open it up, however, and you'll be greeted by a much larger 7.6-inch display. This is the benefit of foldable smartphones: You have access to a mini tablet (sometimes called a "phablet") whenever you want it. That extra screen real estate means you can view single apps in a much larger window, but also run two apps side-by-side. That's a first for any iPhone, even if it's not a first for smartphones in general. And because this is a tablet-like display, your Home Screen looks a bit more like an iPad's, complete with extra widgets and a macOS-like Dock. There's even a Dock on the outer display, and many controls are adjusted to sit on the right of the display to make them accessible using your thumb.

Interestingly, the Duo is the first iPhone in years to lack Face ID. Instead, this device marks the return of Touch ID, integrated into the Side button. (You can also unlock it with your Apple Watch.) It also supports Apple Pencil for the first time on iPhone, and includes two batteries, providing 31 hours of video playback on the inner display, and 44 hours on the outer. You can reach 50% battery in 20 minutes of charging, and five hours of use after five minutes.

It works in many different orientations: You can stand it up tent-style or like a laptop, or fold it slightly to split your keyboard. It also works in StandBy by folding it on its side.

Like the iPhone 18 Pros, the iPhone Duo comes with Apple's new A20 Pro chip. But for the Duo, the chip has a new display engine to power both screens. Apple says it offers up to 35% faster performance than iPhone 17 Pro. While I'm sure it's Apple's fastest chip yet, we'll have to wait until independent benchmarkers put it to the test to know how much better it is than the A19 Pro. The Duo also has Apple's proprietary C2 modem, which provides faster uploads and quicker reconnection to networks.

As noted above, the iPhone Duo has four cameras: two rear cameras and two selfie cameras. Let's start with those rear cameras: Apple has a 48MP fusion lens and a 2x telephoto lens. Some might be sad about the omission of an ultrawide lens. At the same time, the Duo might not be the iPhone for users who care most about mobile photography. Perhaps it'll feel more like the cameras on the iPad: useful to have, but not exactly a selling point. Like the 18 Pro, the Duo supports 4K Time-Lapses and new Photographic Styles.

Perhaps more importantly, the Duo has two selfie cameras: one on the front display, and one on the inner display. This ensures that you can take FaceTime calls and selfies in whichever orientation you have the iPhone Duo in. Crucially, the inner camera is embedded in the display, so you don't ever see it. There are a lot of camera perks with those dual displays: Your subject can see themselves in the outer display; you can stand up the Duo like a tripod; and you can project FaceTime calls on both displays, so everyone can see who you're talking to.

Apple didn't go all out with the colors for the Duo. Buyers will only have two options to choose from here: Star White or Night Sky (dark blue). That's in contrast to the iPhone 18 Pro, which comes in four interesting colors. That said, I'm guessing Apple doesn't expect Duo sales to be affected by color options: Buyers are either going to pay up for the Duo, or they're not, and fun colors probably wouldn't play into that conversation.

Apple's first foldable iPhone doesn't come cheap, of course. The iPhone Duo officially starts at $1,999, which makes this the most expensive iPhone Apple has ever made. And yet, that doesn't sound so bad: Initial reports suggested that the Duo would be more than $2,000, which seemed quite believable considering how RAMaggedon is driving the costs up for all types of tech.

The iPhone Duo can be more expensive, however. $1,999 is the starting price for the 256GB model, though it goes up to 2TB.

While Apple announced the iPhone Duo today, it won't be available right away. Instead, the company says preorders begin Oct. 16, while sales begin Oct. 23. While iPhone preorders are usually a frantic affair, I imagine the Duo's demand will be historic. If you're interested in picking one up as soon as possible, you'll likely want to make sure you preorder it as soon as Apple lets you.

title: Why the iPhone 18 Pro's Variable Aperture Is a Big Development for Smartphone Photography
description: Variable aperture is a huge development for smartphone photography.
fullText:
Every year, Apple claims its newly launched iPhones have the best cameras ever, and those improvements usually revolve around improved sensors, lenses, and software updates. This year, though, there's an unusual camera upgrade that's going to make a massive difference to your photos and videos: The iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max have a variable-aperture lens, a feature unavailable on the much more expensive iPhone Duo. Variable aperture gives you far greater control over lighting in your iPhone photos.

A camera's aperture lets you control how much light reaches the lens. For a brighter photo, you want to let in more light; for a darker one, you'd ideally let in less. This system is similar to the pupils of your eyes, which constrict when the light is too bright and dilate when you suddenly go from bright sunshine to a dark room.

In DSLR cameras, you can see overlapping blades that partially cover the lens. This opening increases or decreases in size depending on the aperture value. This technology is expensive to implement in a smartphone lens, and so far, the improvement in photos hasn't been good enough to justify the investment. That's why it's rare to find the feature in most phones. Apple added variable aperture to its smartphones for the first time with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series. (Note that aperture values are denoted in f-numbers, which means that when you adjust a camera's aperture, the value looks something like f/1.8, f/4.0, etc. The lower the f-number, the brighter the image becomes.)

The iPhone 18 Pro has three rear cameras, but only the main camera offers a variable aperture. It's a 48-megapixel sensor with four aperture f-numbers supported. You can pick an aperture value from f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0m, which should make it significantly easier to get the exposure just right in difficult lighting conditions. You'll also be able to take better photos in low light and try a few additional creative shots with your iPhone 18 Pro. Having a variable aperture is great for controlling depth of field, so you can easily blur the background or keep it in sharp focus when you take photos.

With a larger aperture (f/1.48), you'll be able to reduce the depth of field and blur the background for shots that require focus on a single subject. You can use a smaller aperture (f/4.0) to capture stunning landscapes, where you want the entire photo to be in focus.

If you're thinking that your iPhone already does these things, you're sort of right. But it's worth remembering that up until now, iPhones had to rely on software to perform these tasks, which gets the job done, but the results aren't always exactly what you'd visualize. Having hardware control over aperture gives you greater control over the output and brings the final result much closer to what you visualized. In theory, variable aperture should make the iPhone 18 Pro better for astrophotography, too, but until all of these tasks are tested, it's hard to say how much impact the new feature will have.

The new model will serve as the first big test for John Ternus, who took the role last week

All eyes are on Apple’s annual fall announcement of new products this afternoon, where the company is expected to unveil the most significant change to the iPhone since the smartphone’s introduction in 2007.

Unlike previous iterations, the new iPhone is expected to fold, opening and closing like a passport to double its screen size.

The product release event, titled “Surprise and Shine”, begins at 10am Pacific Standard Time on Apple’s campus in Cupertino, California, south of San Francisco.

While competitors have released foldable smartphones since the late 2010s, the new model will be a first for the iPhone maker and will also serve as the first big test for the company’s new CEO, John Ternus, who assumed the role on 1 September.

Apple is expected to price the phone north of $2000, more than what some of its competitors charge for their foldable phones. A Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, for instance, retails for $1899. Much remains unknown about Apple’s device, including its name, though it is rumored to be named either the iPhone Fold or the iPhone Ultra.

Apple reportedly began testing prototypes of its folding iPhone display in early 2021 – though at the time there were no plans for its launch, according to a Bloomberg report. Ultimately, the phone the company is rumored to launch will be about 5.5in when it’s closed and 7.8in when it opens. It’s also not expected to have Face ID because the device is too thin to hold the camera that would enable the facial recognition scan. Reports indicate it will only offer Touch ID instead.

Apple is also expected to make several more routine announcements, including new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max models. Though the foldable iPhone may take center stage Wednesday, demand for foldable phones makes up only a small sliver of overall mobile device sales. Customers’ interest in standard iPhones, by contrast, remains high, as evidenced in Apple’s most recent robust earnings.

The company is also expected to unveil new iterations of some of its other product offerings at its events and over the next few months, including updates to its Apple Watch and AirPods lines, according to Bloomberg, as well as its first-ever touchscreen MacBook.

Ternus will take the stage as CEO for the first time and mark the beginning of his tenure as the head of Apple, replacing outgoing CEO Tim Cook. In a note to employees on his first day, Ternus said that he was excited about “the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined”.

“I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store,” Ternus wrote in his letter. “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible.”

title: Five Devices I Expect Apple to Announce on Wednesday
description: Apple will announce its first-ever foldable iPhone tomorrow.
fullText:
Apple has a big event scheduled for tomorrow. On Wednesday, Sept. 9, at 1 p.m. ET, the company will take the virtual stage to announce a series of new products. Exactly what those products are, only Apple knows for sure. But thanks to leaks and rumors, we generally know what some of those updates are going to be. I'm confident we'll see these five devices announced tomorrow, though Apple may have other updates in store for us as well.

The defining product announcement for Apple tomorrow will be the iPhone Ultra. The Ultra is Apple's first foldable iPhone, undeniably the biggest update to the iPhone line in years (or, perhaps, ever). Like other foldables, the iPhone Ultra will feature a "smaller" display when closed (perhaps 5.5 inches), and will open to reveal a larger display within (rumors suggest 7.8 inches). Leaks suggest the devices will have two rear cameras in addition to a selfie cam, though it may use Touch ID rather than Face ID.

Apple will likely debut its new A20 chip with all its new iPhones this year, Ultra included. The company may pack in 12GB of RAM and a larger battery to accommodate the dual displays—perhaps 5,000 mAh or 5,500, per the rumors. While we won't know for sure until we see it, leaks suggest Apple has managed to reduce the appearance of the Ultra's "crease," or where the display folds in. If so, the Ultra could have one of the better-looking foldable displays on the market, but, again, we won't know until tomorrow.

While most of the iPhone Ultra's specs are exciting, one thing is anything but: its price. A foldable iPhone was always doomed to be expensive, but thanks to the ongoing memory crisis, all tech is pricier than ever. Rumors suggest the iPhone Ultra will start at more than $2,000. As of this article, Apple's most expensive iPhone is the $2,000 2TB iPhone 17 Pro Max, but even it has a starting price of $1,199 for 256GB.

Apple isn't doing away with its traditional iPhone design. On the contrary, the other iPhones Apple is expected to announce tomorrow, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, will be small updates from last year's iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max. (As an owner of the latter, I'm happy I don't have much pressure to upgrade.)

Here's what's new from last year: According to the rumors, the iPhone 18 Pro line may ship with slightly smaller Dynamic Islands than before. While you'll still see the camera cutout, it won't be quite as prominent as on the iPhone 17 Pro series, which gives you a bit more screen real estate to work with. In addition, the new devices may get cameras with variable apertures, as opposed to the fixed apertures in the 17 Pros. That would allow the 18 Pros to take in more light in dark environments, like how many traditional cameras work. Like the iPhone Ultra, the iPhone 18 Pros will likely get the A20 chip, so unless Apple has made any major breakthroughs here, expect the usual slight increase in performance and efficiency. The 18 Pro could also ship with Apple's C2 modem, which may offer more privacy benefits in addition to cellular performance.

Rumors also suggest the 18 Pro and 19 Pro Max batteries could be larger and more efficient, but since Apple is private about its battery specs, we'll have to wait for independent teardown videos to know for sure. What most of us will be happy to see, however, are the new colors. While the 18 Pro should look almost identical to the 17 Pro, you'll have color choices like dark cherry and sky blue, and likely at least one more option: either black, light gray, or both. Like the Ultra, the 18 Pro will likely cost more than ever this year. The base model may ship at $1,299, while the 18 Pro Max may start at $1,399. Once you start bumping up the storage, the price may only increase.

That's it for iPhones, at least if the rumors can be believed. Apple may push other iPhones, like the iPhone 18, 18e, and iPhone Air 2, into the spring of 2027, but if they do, it isn't clear whether they'll punt the entire announcement or simply share that these phones will be available next year. (My money's on the latter.)

Apple's next-generation Apple Watch is likely coming tomorrow, too. The Apple Watch Series 12 might not change much from the Series 11, but rumors point to three key updates. First, as expected, there's a new "S-series" chip, the S11. While there isn't much out there on performance, it will be Apple's first Apple Watch chip released during its big AI push, so, presumably, it will help power some of those new features. Turning to health, the Series 12 may bring an "always-on" heart-rate sensor, similar to what you can find from WHOOP, which could give you more health data than the current watches.

Finally, Apple may bring back the ceramic watch option this year in two colors: white and dark gray. We don't have much pricing info yet, but when Apple released the ceramic Series 5, it started at $1,299, so that option could get quite expensive in our RAMaggedon era.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is also light on rumors. From what I see, leakers expect an Ultra that looks much like the Ultra 3, with similar upgrades to the Series 12. That means the S12 chip and an always-on heart-rate sensor. While I expect to see the Ultra 4 tomorrow, I don't expect it to be an overhauled device.

While the above five products are almost guaranteed to debut tomorrow, other devices aren't so locked in. As MacRumors highlights, Apple has some other products in the works that may or may not make it to its big September event. They include a new Apple TV 4K with an upgraded chip, a new HomePod mini with a faster processor, and, most notably, the "Home hub," which would be Apple's first smart-home display. That device could come with a seven-inch screen, a camera, motion sensors, and more, capable of running Siri AI, making video calls, and streaming content. Apple could also release fifth-generation AirPods with the H3 chip, but we'll have to wait until tomorrow to know for sure.

Apple will also likely take tomorrow to confirm release dates for its upcoming slate of software updates, including iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, and watchOS 27. If you have a compatible iPhone, iPad, Mac, or Apple Watch, you'll be able to install the updates for free whenever Apple drops them.

title: 10 Apple Health Hacks Every iPhone User Should Know
description: You don't need an Apple Watch to get great health insights from Apple.
fullText:
Even if you’ve never opened the Apple Health app, if you have an iPhone, you’ve probably used apps that send information to its on-phone database. Apple Health is a powerful tool for controlling who gets access to your health data, logging data in different ways, and even taking at-home screening tests for certain health issues. If you have an Apple Watch, that’s great, but you don’t need one (or any wearable!) to take advantage of most of these 10 hacks to get more out of the Apple Health app.

Before we get into the other hacks, I’d like to discuss just how private your Apple Health data is (or isn’t). Apple provides its Health privacy policy here, and it says that your data lives on your own device and is encrypted when your phone is locked. There are some exceptions, though, which you can turn on or off. Here are the main things you may want to check on:

Individual apps can ask for permission to read data from Apple Health. (They also need your permission to write data to it.) You can control per-app permissions in Settings. Or, for a specific data point (like “walking and running distance”), go to that area of Apple Health and tap Data Sources and Access.

You can back up your health data via iCloud, which means it will live on Apple’s servers so you can access it from any of your devices. It is encrypted so Apple cannot read it. Manage this from your iCloud settings (in Settings, under your name).

You can share health data with your doctor or with people you know, like family members. To manage who has access, go to the Health app and tap the Sharing tab.

During workouts, some data from your workout may appear in a Live Activity widget on your lock screen. To hide this data while your phone is locked, go to the Settings app, tap Face ID & Passcode, and then under Allow Access When Locked, toggle Workout Health Data.

Your Medical ID may be available when your device is locked. (This is how bystanders and first responders can access your emergency contact or other information you’d like to remain available in emergencies.) To control access to this, go to the Health app, find Medical ID, and toggle Show When Locked.

The Health app includes a built-in medication tracker with a number of hidden features. Browse or search for Medications, and set up tracking by adding a medication, or anything else. You can type in the name, or use your camera to scan the bottle’s label. (This also works for over-the-counter meds and supplements, like if you want to be sure to take a vitamin every day.) I like that you can customize a pill-shaped icon to match a pill’s appearance.

Next, you can set up reminders. From this screen, you can tell the app when you plan to take your medication (if it’s one you take regularly, rather than as needed). The Health app will notify you at that time. To make the most of this feature, I recommend setting up follow-up reminders, which you’ll find on a different screen as well—more about that below.

After you set up your medications, scroll to the bottom of the medications screen and tap Pin to Summary. Now you just have to open the Health app and tap Medications to see a list of what you need to take today. You can also log via Siri, including batched logging like “Siri, log that I took my 10 a.m. meds” so you don’t have to list each one.

At the bottom of the Medications screen, you can tap Options and turn on Follow Up Reminders, which will give you an extra notification 30 minutes after the first one if you haven’t logged a dose. I use this feature all the time myself: I get the first reminder while I’m in the middle of doing something, eventually take the pill, then the follow-up reminds me to log it. If I got distracted along the way, I have a second chance to not miss a dose.

Another handy feature here is the Export PDF button at the bottom of the page, which will print out a list of all your current medications so you can bring it to your medical appointments or anywhere else you need to.

If you’re not familiar with the Health app, you might not think there’s much there—just a few things on the home screen. You can change that, but it takes a few steps. You see, rather than being a minimalist app, there’s so much available in Health that Apple figures it’s not worth giving you a big list to start off. Tap the magnifying glass icon in the lower right corner, and you’ll see a whole list of categories. You can search from this screen, or browse the categories.

Definitely take a minute to browse through these and see what features you might actually use. If you track what you eat in an Apple Health-connected app, you’ll be able to see all the individual components here: how much protein you’ve gotten today, for instance. Anything that a wearable can track is on here, including things you probably didn’t realize. I have a grade for my walking steadiness, for example.

Once you’ve figured out which of these hundreds of data points are actually useful, put the ones you care about on the main app screen (called Summary). Find a relevant card by searching or browsing, scroll to the bottom, and tap Pin to Summary. This way you can see exactly what you want when you open the app: say, your steps, protein intake, and the day’s medications. (Plus a few things you may want to add after you learn about them below...)

A lot of us are nervous about logging reproductive health data anywhere that may not be private. I’ve written that Euki may be the best standalone app for privacy, but you don’t need to use an app at all: Tracking directly in Apple Health means that your data is encrypted and lives on your phone, subject to the privacy features discussed above.

To use the built-in tracker, go to the magnifying glass and tap (or search for) Cycle Tracking. The cycle tracker on this screen (which you can pin to your summary) allows you to log menstrual bleeding, as well as “factors” like contraceptive use, pregnancy, and more.

Under the Options at the bottom of this screen, you can turn on period predictions, fertile window estimates, and more. I recommend enabling the Symptoms log if you’d like to keep track of things like cramps and nausea. You can also decide if you want Apple Health to use your temperature and heart rate data from a wearable for better cycle detection.

Another surprising use for manual logging in the Health app is under Mental Wellbeing. This is a really useful screen, since it collects things known to affect mental health, like your sleep, exercise minutes, time in daylight, and more. From here, you can also set up emotion and mood logging. The app explains that it considers emotions to be how you feel right now, and moods are how you’ve felt overall that day.

You can turn on reminders to log your moods. The default is to log twice per day: once around midday, and once at the end of the day. Scroll to the bottom of the Mental Wellbeing screen to set up logging.  Once you’ve set it up, it will appear as State of Mind; you may want to pin this to your summary. You can even view graphs of your state of mind over time, and see what other factors they associate with. A really useful view is to tap Show in Charts and then highlight Life Factors so you can see if your moods seem to track your exercise minutes or your hours of sleep.

The Health app also includes a built-in hearing test, but it requires AirPods Pro 3 (or AirPods Pro 2). To find the hearing test, look up Hearing in the Health app, then Get More From Health, and then Take Hearing Test. This will only be available if you have the right type of headphones connected. Follow the prompts to take the test. Apple has more information on this test here. If your results seem concerning, you can export a PDF of your results to discuss with a professional.

Accessing your medical records through patient portals can be annoying. Instead, you can import your digital medical records directly into the Health app, giving you quick access to your medical history as needed. Apple offers a list of the healthcare systems whose data it can access.

It’s worth looking over the privacy policies for this feature as well, but the good news is that the data follows an encrypted connection between your phone and the healthcare organization, without ever giving Apple (the company) access to it. I’d recommend turning off Improve Health Records, which sends an anonymized version of your data to Apple; health records are detailed information about your body—but feel free to leave it on if that’s your preference. You can back up your health data over iCloud, as discussed above.

As with menstrual cycle tracking, it can be useful to any health data directly in the app. You can actually do this with just about any data point: just view that type of data, and then tap the plus sign in the upper right corner. Think you took about 1,000 steps when you had your watch off? Just tap the plus on the Steps screen and add them.

A handy place to use this feature is for blood pressure tracking. Some wearables estimate your blood pressure, like Whoop and the Samsung Galaxy Watch. But you don’t need one of those to log your numbers: just take note of your blood pressure at the doctor’s office, or when you use a wrist cuff or one of those machines they sometimes have at pharmacies. Open Blood Pressure and tap the plus, then put in the new reading. You’ll be able to view your history of blood pressure readings, and even see charts of how it has changed over time.

Some medications affect your heart rate, most notably beta blockers and calcium channel blockers. If you’re taking one of those, your heart rate won’t match Apple’s general-purpose formulas for gauging your cardio fitness (a VO2max estimate) from your heart rate. You’ll appear to have a higher cardio fitness than you actually have.

To let Apple account for this, go to your profile picture, tap Health Details, tap Edit at the top of the page, and scroll down to Medications That Affect Heart Rate. You can select calcium channel blockers or beta blockers, or both; these are the only categories of medication that Apple can account for.

There’s a Medical ID feature that can be accessed from your lock screen even without unlocking your phone. It’s a great place to put your emergency contact information, but to make the most use of it, you need the people in your life to know how to access the information and what’s in there.

I first learned about the Medical ID when I was teaching a class. A student came up to tell me about a medical condition, and showed me how to access her Medical ID (it’s right at the bottom of the lock screen). Most importantly, she made sure I knew what information I’d be able to find there, so I knew when and whether to reach for it in an emergency.

I’d advise that you do the same if you want to be prepared. Besides allergies and contact information, the Medical ID field can include information on whether you’re pregnant, what medications you take, any medical conditions you’d like to disclose, and your height, weight, and blood type. There’s also an area at the bottom for notes, where you can add any information you feel is critical.

Also consider whether you want to turn on Share During Emergency Call, which allows this information to be shared with emergency services. You can also control whether or not your Medical ID appears on your lock screen using a separate toggle.

title: We Now Know When Apple's Big iPhone Event Will Happen
description: Get ready for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra.
fullText:
You don't need to follow leaks and rumors to know that Apple will announce the iPhone 18 next month. The company has revealed new iPhones once a year every year since its first smartphone launch back in 2007. The real unknown, of course, is what day exactly Apple will make these announcements. As of Wednesday, we know for sure.

Ahead of the event, make sure to enter Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game. The quiz is now in its third round, and each correct guess gets you the chance to win the latest Apple Watch.

Apple has set an official time and date for its iPhone 18 announcement. The company is scheduled to kick off its keynote on Wednesday, Sept. 9 at 10 a.m. PT. While Apple is inviting some media members to attend in person, anyone can watch the presentation live online. Apple's senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak, confirmed the keynote in a post on X:

We don't know for sure what Apple will reveal on Sept. 9, but leaks and rumors give us some good guesses. The math tells us that Apple will go from the iPhone 17 to the iPhone 18 this year, while the leaks suggest that we'll see the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the foldable "iPhone Ultra."(Apple may delay the standard iPhone 18 to 2027, per rumors.)

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will likely be standard upgrades from the iPhone 17 Pro series: Expect better cameras, bigger batteries, new colors (including the new "light blue" and "dark cherry"), the new A20 chip, and higher price tags. The star of the show will be Apple's first foldable iPhone, which will come with many of the same internals as the iPhone 18 Pros, but may ship with Touch ID instead of Face ID, and, of course, with two display types: a smaller outer display, which opens up to reveal a larger inner display. This might be Apple's most expensive iPhone yet, fetching over $2,000, but we'll have to wait and see once Apple officially announces its price tag.

title: 10 Hacks Every iOS 27 User Should Know
description: These 10 hacks are essential for anyone upgrading to iOS 27.
fullText:
If you have an iPhone 11 or newer (including the second-gen iPhone SE), you can look forward to installing iOS 27 in the fall. Apple's next big update is heavy on the AI and stability upgrades, and will likely drop sometime in September. However, iOS 27 has also been available in beta all summer. I've been running the update on my primary iPhone for nearly three months now, and during that time, I've discovered a bunch of hacks I think every iOS 27 user should know. Whether you're installing the update today or next month, you should definitely try out these useful hacks for your iPhone.

Apple introduced Liquid Glass with iOS 26, and didn't hold back with its design choices. While some liked the changes, others have criticized Liquid Glass for focusing more on style over substance. In response, cApple introduced new ways to adjust and customize the design's transparency effects. That only continues with iOS 27. There's now a new slider that lets you reduce or almost eliminate the Liquid Glass effect. You can find it under Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass in iOS 27. Move the slider towards the right to improve readability.

I've lost count of the number of times I've accidentally sent incomprehensible voice notes to people on iMessage. In my case, the culprit was the audio message button to the right of the text box in the Messages app. Luckily, in iOS 27, you can either change that button to dictation, or remove it altogether. To change it up, head over to Settings > Apps > Messages, and select Show in Text Field. You can pick one of these three choices: Record Audio, Start Dictation, and None. The last one (None) removes the audio message button from the text box. Note that you can still access the "Audio" option from the (+) menu, while dictation will appear in your keyboard.

With iOS 27, Apple is making it possible to set different volume levels for ringtones, alerts, and alarms. If you want to silence app notifications and texts, but still hear your ringtones and alarms, this one's for you. To set it up, go to Settings > Sounds & Haptics, and turn off Match Ringtone Volume under "Alarms and Timers." You can now use the slider to set a different volume level for those two features. Similarly, you can turn off Match Ringtone Volume under "Alerts and System Sounds," and move the slider according to your needs.

iOS 27 introduces a convenient new slider that lets you set timers from the Dynamic Island on your iPhone. To use it directly from the Lock Screen, however, you'll have to remove one of the two controls already present. Pick up your iPhone, and allow Face ID to unlock the device without leaving the Lock Screen. Now, tap and hold the screen, then tap Customize near the base of the display. Tap the "-" button next to the two controls near the bottom-right and bottom-left corners of the display. By default, these two controls are for the flashlight and camera, respectively. After deleting one control, press the + button that appears in its place, and select Timer from the list of controls. Tap the Done button in the top-right corner. Now, when you tap this button, you'll see a slider appear from the Dynamic Island up top. Move the slider to set a timer, and tap Start Timer to get it going.

With iOS 27, you can essentially start a livestream from FaceTime for the people you're calling. A new feature called "Dual Capture" allows you to record and stream video from both the front camera and the rear camera simultaneously. This means that you can show your face and the things around you during a FaceTime call, so you don't have to pick one or the other at any given moment.

To use this feature, start a FaceTime video call with another person, and tap the "Flip" button that appears in your selfie video frame. This will start a Dual Capture session. You can stop streaming both cameras by tapping the Flip button in the bottom-left corner of the screen, which returns you to a regular selfie video. In addition, you can turn off the front camera feed in a FaceTime call. When in Dual Capture mode, tap the button that appears in the top-left corner of your front camera feed, the icon with a crossed-out person. This turns off the front camera stream, and lets you show just the feed off the rear camera. Note that Dual Capture is limited to iPhone Air, iPhone 17 series, and newer devices.

If you or your gym has GymKit-compatible equipment, you can connect your Apple Watch to the machines to track your workouts. I use this feature all the time, but, of course, if I forget to wear my Apple Watch, or if it runs out of charge, then my workouts don't get logged. Apple is fixing this problem by bringing GymKit compatibility to iPhones. With iOS 27, you'll be able to connect your iPhone directly to compatible treadmills, elliptical machines, indoor bikes, and other cardio equipment. Whether you don't have an Apple Watch, or don't have access to it, you can continue tracking your workouts with greater levels of accuracy.

Setup is easy: As explained by 9to5Mac, you can tap your iPhone against a GymKit-enabled machine, like a treadmill, then follow the on-screen instructions to set up and track a workout, such as "Indoor Run" or "Indoor Walk." All data is removed from the machine at the end of the session, and stored directly on your iPhone. Note that this feature won't necessarily track your heart rate. However, if you have a pair of AirPods Pro 3, you can use the built-in heart rate sensor to track your workout.

If you're tired of typos when you're dictating something to your iPhone, use iOS 27's "Advanced Dictation Preview." The new feature uses Siri AI to upgrade dictation's accuracy, and polishes text automatically—similar to Google's Rambler feature. Apple says Siri AI's dictation is now capable of "automatically handling capitalization, punctuation, and formatting" as speak, though you need to enable it manually. Advanced Dictation Preview is only available to iPhones that support Siri AI's most powerful features, including the iPhone 17 Pro series and iPhone Air. You can enable it by going to Settings > General > Keyboard > Advanced Dictation Preview.

iOS 27 has a hidden macOS-like recovery mode, which allows you to diagnose and fix software problems without using a computer. Once you're running iOS 27 on your iPhone, you can access it with the following key presses:

Press Volume Down and release it.

Hold the Side Button (power button) till you see "Loading recovery options…" on the screen.

Note that recovery mode should be a last resort to fix your iPhone, and you should not try it without understanding the risks. More than one option in recovery mode directly formats your iPhone and erases all your data, so proceed with extreme caution.

iOS 27 introduces extra-large widgets, which take up almost all of the available screen space on your device. This allows you to view all of your calendar events in a single widget. (Finally.) To try this in iOS 27, hold an empty part of the Home Screen on your iPhone, and tap the paintbrush icon in the top-right corner. Search for "Calendar," and swipe right till you see the biggest widgets. At the time of writing, Calendar offers two of these extra-large widgets: "Up Next," and "List." Hit Add Widget to drop it to your Home Screen. You can also try other extra-large widgets such as Smart Stack, Music, and other apps that support this iOS 27 feature.

Find My allows you to share your location with your loved ones, but it can sometimes feel a bit invasive. To temporarily stop sharing your location, you could turn off your phone's GPS, but that affects all other apps which rely on location sharing features. iOS 27 has a more elegant solution, which allows you to temporarily stop sharing your location with others. To use it, open Find My, go to the People tab, and tap the three dots next to a contact's name. Under "My Location," select Hide Location, which will turn off location sharing for a day.

ChatGPT Can Now Control iMessage, Potentially Raising Apple Privacy Concerns
description: OpenAI rolled out support on Thursday for controlling Apple Inc.’s iMessage service via ChatGPT, a move with the potential to raise privacy concerns for the iPhone maker.
fullText:
(Bloomberg) -- OpenAI rolled out support on Thursday for controlling Apple Inc.'s iMessage service via ChatGPT, a move with the potential to raise privacy concerns for the iPhone maker.

China Sentences Evergrande's Hui to Life for 'Heinous' Crime

Bessent Deploys Debt Buybacks in Sign of Concern Over Yield Rise

US 30-Year Bonds Reverse Gains From Treasury's Buyback Surprise

US Set to Cut Tariffs on Canada Metals, Autos in Trade Deal

Natalie Harp, Trump's Gatekeeper, Is at Center of Senator Jon Ossoff Clash

The new feature, available for ChatGPT on the Mac, allows the OpenAI system to take actions such as reading, writing and sending text messages. It also can search through messages and get summaries and other information about conversations from the Apple Messages app.

Apple has positioned itself as a staunch privacy advocate, and it's protective about the contents of users' messages. An OpenAI tool that could upload Apple customer data to that company's network is likely to spark questions.

An Apple representative didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

The move comes at a time of broader tension between the two companies. Apple sued OpenAI last month, accusing the AI provider of stealing information about upcoming products.

In response to questions about the new feature, OpenAI stressed that it requires a user's consent and doesn't create an index of all someone's messages. The plug-in also runs locally on the Mac and uses existing operating system tools, such as AppleScript and Accessibility, to work with the Messages app, OpenAI said.

There are several opt-in menus in both the ChatGPT app and Apple's own operating system about the tie-in. When a user first sets up the integration, a permissions screen appears in ChatGPT that says the computer's on-device message history will be accessed by the app.

Users are also required to change privacy-related preferences within the Mac's System Settings app. That includes enabling a feature named Full Disk Access. Moreover, users need to give ChatGPT permission to access the names of contacts and automation tools. It's similar to the settings that need to be enabled to turn on popular AI-based automation software like Codex Computer Use.

OpenAI recently rolled out support for analyzing information in a user's iPhone and iPad Health app, but Apple's iOS and iPadOS operating systems have a feature that requires customers to specifically approve their data being given to ChatGPT.

ChatGPT already works with other Mac apps, including the Xcode programming suite, Notes and Terminal, though those tie-ins are less likely to upset Apple's privacy managers and marketing teams than an unofficial Messages integration.

title: Six Emergency Features You Should Enable on Your iPhone
description: These iOS settings make sure you can get help when you need it.
fullText:
We all carry our phones everywhere—which means your device is a lifeline in the event of an emergency. Apple has a host of built-in features on iOS to facilitate getting help when it's needed, and you should take the time to turn on these critical settings on your iPhone (and know how to use them) before an emergency happens.

If you're ever in an accident or experience an emergency in which you're unable to communicate, you will likely want first responders to have quick access to important medical information, such as allergies, medications, and health conditions. You can enter all of this into your Medical ID in the Health app and add a shortcut to your lock screen so responders can see it even if they can't unlock your device.

In the Health app, tap your profile picture and go to Medical ID. Add any relevant information about your health, including your blood type and any detailed notes. Toggle on Show When Locked—this will allow responders to pull up the information from your iPhone passcode screen via Emergency > Medical ID. You can also enable Share During Emergency Call, which will share your Medical ID if you call or text emergency services.

While you're filling out your Medical ID, enter at least one emergency contact. Click Edit > Add Emergency Contact and select from your existing Contacts list. Tap the contact to add the relationship, such as a spouse or parent. There are also options for unrelated individuals like manager, teacher, social worker, or daycare. Your emergency contacts will be visible to first responders with your Medical ID. Your iPhone can also send a message to your contacts as part of Crash Detection and Emergency SOS, which we'll get into below.

If you're using Focus modes that silence notifications, you may still want to receive alerts from people you're close to in the event of an emergency—for example, your kid's school (or your actual kid). Emergency Bypass allows sounds and vibrations to break through even when your device is on silent. Emergency contacts in your Medical ID get this treatment by default, but you can enable it for others independently in their individual contact card. Tap Edit > Ringtone/Text Tone and toggle Emergency Bypass on.

Emergency SOS is a long-standing iPhone feature that allows you to quickly call or text emergency services (and, if you're in the U.S., share your Medical ID when doing so). You don't specifically need to enable it, but you can change the mechanism for initiating the call under Settings > Emergency SOS and switch the toggle next to Call with Hold and Release and/or Call with 5 Button Presses. You can also initiate an emergency call from your iPhone passcode screen and text emergency services from Messages.

You can also use Emergency SOS via satellite if you're out of service. This newer feature connects you to the closest first responders wherever you are, and it is only available when there's no cellular or wifi connection. If your call won't connect, tap Emergency Text via Satellite > Report Emergency and follow the prompts. Your device will send information to responders, such as your location, remaining iPhone battery life, and Medical ID. Ensure location sharing for Emergency Calls & SOS is on under Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services > System Services. For the time being, Emergency SOS via satellite is free, though it's not available worldwide. Satellite is also available for requesting roadside assistance in the U.S., UK, and Australia.

Crash Detection is an iPhone and Apple Watch feature that can call emergency services and alert your emergency contacts if your vehicle has been in a severe crash, such as a collision or rollover. You'll hear an alarm and get a display alert on your device with an emergency call slider, and you can either complete the call or dismiss the alert if you don't need emergency services. If you don't do either within 10 seconds, your device will automatically make the call after another 30-second countdown. It will also send your location to your emergency contacts and display a Medical ID slider for emergency responders, which is why it's important to set both of these up. Crash detection is on by default, but you can turn it off under Settings > Emergency SOS.

Your iPhone can also notify you when there are safety issues, extreme weather, or other critical incidents in your area. You don't actually need to turn these on, as government alerts—public safety, emergency, and AMBER—are enabled by default, but you should ensure yours are active under Settings > Notifications (scroll all the way to the bottom). Click into the Enhance Safety Alerts menu for additional settings for earthquake and "imminent threat" alerts, which may include supplemental alerts for floods and other natural disasters.

title: MirrorSpeaker – Use your Windows PC as an iPhone speaker
description: Use a Windows 11 PC as an iPhone Bluetooth speaker or AirPlay screen receiver. - codyabraham/MirrorSpeaker
fullText:
MirrorSpeaker is a small Windows desktop app that turns a PC into an AirPlay screen receiver or an iPhone Bluetooth speaker. It uses Windows' built-in Bluetooth audio receiver for phone-only video apps such as TikTok, and gives UxPlay a simple native interface for AirPlay mirroring.

Privacy policy · Security policy ·
Code signing policy · MIT license

The public source repository is
github.com/codyabraham/MirrorSpeaker.

The mirrored video opens in a separate GStreamer window managed by UxPlay. Keeping the media renderer separate is the most reliable Windows configuration supported by the upstream receiver.

The public source build requires Windows 11 and the .NET 10 LTS SDK. From
PowerShell in this folder:

The published app is framework-dependent and does not bundle Microsoft .NET or
WPF runtime binaries. Running dist\win-x64\MirrorSpeaker.exe requires the
Microsoft .NET 10 Desktop Runtime (x64) to be installed.

With the pinned Inno Setup 7.0.2 installed, create the per-user Windows
installer, portable ZIP, and SHA-256 checksum file with:

The outputs are written below artifacts\release. The installer adds Start
Menu and desktop shortcuts, registers a normal Windows uninstaller, and
supports Inno Setup's silent switches. It first checks for a compatible
Microsoft .NET 10 Desktop Runtime (x64). If that runtime is missing, setup
clearly prompts the user, downloads only the pinned official Microsoft
10.0.10 x64 runtime, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and runs Microsoft's
runtime installer. An Internet connection and administrator approval for that
Microsoft system prerequisite may therefore be required; MirrorSpeaker itself
remains a per-user installation. The pinned runtime-installer SHA-256 is
e82fc901c8f52d716293b2bc0830ce0dd254a06268c457a19e8fc503560a84d1.

The portable ZIP does not download or bundle .NET. Its
MirrorSpeaker.exe requires the Microsoft .NET 10 Desktop Runtime (x64) to be
installed before launch. The ZIP uses portable.flag so MirrorSpeaker settings
and pairing records stay with the extracted app.

The first public release intentionally does not redistribute a prebuilt
receiver engine. AirPlay setup remains an explicit, user-initiated local
source build. A future release may include a pruned, versioned receiver
package built by scripts\Build-ReceiverPackage.ps1 only after the receiver
has a reproducible public CI build, complete corresponding source, and an
explicit license and legal review. The internal-test override and its
artifacts are never publishable. See
docs/RELEASING.md for the complete signing, licensing,
silent-install, and clean-Windows test checklist.

For TikTok or normal iPhone audio, choose Bluetooth speaker — best for TikTok. MirrorSpeaker checks Windows' Bluetooth-device records first, selects an already-connected iPhone, and reuses it without pairing again. Connected beside the phone describes its general Bluetooth link; only the Bluetooth connected status badge confirms that Windows also opened the separate audio receiver profile. If that profile does not open, MirrorSpeaker reports a failure and this PC will not appear as an iPhone audio destination yet. If the iPhone is not listed, click Bluetooth settings, confirm Windows shows it, return to MirrorSpeaker, and click Refresh phones. Bluetooth mode needs neither the AirPlay engine nor a Private Wi-Fi network or firewall exception.

AirPlay requires the iPhone and PC on the same local network. Guest Wi-Fi, VPNs, access-point/client isolation, or VLAN separation can block AirPlay discovery.

For TikTok, use Bluetooth speaker — best for TikTok. TikTok may treat AirPlay screen mirroring as external playback and stop its local picture. Bluetooth avoids that AirPlay classification. Windows does not expose codec or buffer controls for this receiver API, so a small wireless delay remains. Using another wireless headset or speaker creates two radio hops and can be less reliable than the PC's built-in speakers or wired headphones. MirrorSpeaker keeps an enabled receiver alive after a transient Windows opening failure, recognizes a later phone-initiated connection, and makes bounded background attempts to open or recover the audio link.

The smoke tests cover safe argument construction, port validation, receiver log/PIN interpretation, engine discovery, settings persistence, and wireless-output classification. A physical iPhone is required for end-to-end Bluetooth audio validation; AirPlay mirroring also requires a local Wi-Fi network.

MirrorSpeaker has no telemetry or project-operated cloud service. The screen
stream travels directly from the iPhone to the PC over the local network.
Pairing is enabled by default, and the provided firewall rules apply only to
Private networks. The AirPlay receiver and its dependencies connect to the
network only for the user-requested operations described in the
privacy policy. Please report vulnerabilities privately as
described in the security policy.

MirrorSpeaker has not yet been accepted into the SignPath Foundation
open-source program. Current builds are unsigned and must not be represented
as signed. If the project is accepted, official Windows releases will use:

Free code signing provided by SignPath.io, certificate by SignPath Foundation

metadata. A future SignPath signature would instead show SignPath Foundation
as the Authenticode certificate signer; the two fields have different
purposes. See the complete code signing policy.

MirrorSpeaker's original C# and XAML controller code is open source under the
MIT License. The user-initiated receiver setup obtains and locally
builds the pinned UxPlay revision recorded in
scripts/Install-ReceiverEngine.ps1;
UxPlay is GPL-3.0. UxPlay-derived source fragments and patch payloads embedded
in that script are GPL-3.0 material and are not covered by MirrorSpeaker's
root MIT license.

UxPlay also warns that the legal status of its third-party GPL PlayFair
library for handling FairPlay is unclear. MirrorSpeaker repeats that warning
without making a legal determination or representing that redistribution has
been approved. This is one reason the first public release must omit the
prebuilt receiver binary.

The framework-dependent application does not redistribute Microsoft .NET or
WPF runtime binaries. The normal Windows installer can obtain the pinned
Microsoft .NET 10 Desktop Runtime prerequisite directly from Microsoft when it
is missing; the portable ZIP requires that runtime to be installed separately.
The application does include Microsoft's unmodified Windows SDK .NET projection
assemblies needed to call the Windows Bluetooth APIs; their Windows SDK terms
and the remaining SignPath System Library review are disclosed in the
third-party notices.
The user-initiated receiver setup obtains GStreamer and MSYS2 locally, and the
Windows setup and uninstall programs contain Inno Setup-generated code. Each
third-party component remains governed by its respective license. See

title: Firefox Can Now Block Ads on iOS (but You Have to Enable It)
description: The new feature will block most (but not all) ads.
fullText:
Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device. Mozilla is slowly rolling out native ad blocking, which you can enable once the tool is available on your account.

According to Mozilla's support page detailing the new feature, Firefox will block third-party ad networks and exchanges along with many third-party ads served on websites at the network level. It will also block ad-related trackers, pop-ups, and overlays. The platform is still letting some ads through, though: For example, you'll still see ads in search results from engines like Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo, as well as sponsored content on the Firefox Home and New Tab pages. There may also be ads that aren't covered by the EasyList filter list.

Of course, Firefox isn't the only browser to natively block ads on iOS. For example, both DuckDuckGo and Brave have built-in ad blocking in their mobile apps and also allow you to disable their own search ads. Note that ad-blocking functionality doesn't extend outside of the Firefox iOS app, but URL filters in iOS 26, along with a third-party app like Wipr 2, can block ads in other apps.

Ad blocking in Firefox will be off by default. To enable it, open the iOS app, tap the three dots, and go to Settings > Browsing. Under the Content header, toggle on Ad Blocker. You can do this from the Site menu by tapping Ad Blocker (underneath the site name and URL), which will open the Browsing menu directly. The site menu will show you at a glance whether ad blocking is on or off.

Firefox says this feature is currently "experimental," meaning it hasn't yet been made available to all users, so you may not see these options in your browser settings.

title: 10 Screenshot Hacks Every iPhone User Should Know
description: Taking a screenshot on your iPhone can be so much more than just pressing two buttons.
fullText:
While the Mac has the best screenshot tools of any Apple device, it's not quite the same story on iPhone. Your iOS device is mostly restricted to built-in tools for taking screenshots and screen recordings, which makes it hard to bypass apps that block those features. Having said that, your iPhone's screenshot tool is anything but basic, supporting editing, annotations, and even extracting text from images. If you want to take better screenshots on iOS, these 10 hacks can help.

I've always found it unintuitive to take screenshots using hardware buttons on a device with a touchscreen. There are two easy ways to avoid pressing those buttons to take screenshots. The first one relies on a virtual Home button, which you can enable by going to Settings > Accessibility > Touch > AssistiveTouch. From here, enable AssistiveTouch to add a virtual Home button to your iPhone. Next, tap Customize Top Level Menu, then, if you're only interested in using this option for screenshots, reduce the number of icons from six to one by tapping the minus button. From here, tap the remaining icon on this settings page. Go to Device > Screenshot, and tap the blue checkmark in the top-right corner. The next time you tap the virtual Home button, your iPhone will immediately take a screenshot.

The second method uses Back Tap, an iOS feature that triggers various actions when you physically tap the back of your iPhone. You can enable this by going to Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Back Tap. Select either Double Tap or Triple Tap, and go to Device > Screenshot. I recommend picking Triple Tap to avoid accidental screenshots. Once you enable this, tap the back of your phone thrice to take screenshots.

When someone sends you a screenshot of a ticket, or if you've saved an image that mentions a date or time, you can add it to your calendar with a hidden iOS feature. Once you open the screenshot, tap the small Live Text button in the bottom-right corner. (Its icon has three horizontal lines surrounded by dotted borders.) This will reveal a date or time in the bottom-left corner of the screenshot. Tap that button, and you'll see a new page where you can quickly add the event to your calendar. Sometimes, you may see a "More" button next to the identified date or time. This appears when there are multiple dates in a screenshot, and you can tap "More" to select the correct one for your calendar entry. Your iPhone can also identify flight numbers in screenshots and show you the current status of that flight.

This is one of the best features for people who want to avoid piling up useless screenshots in their photo libraries. Once you capture a screenshot on your iPhone, tap the thumbnail to open the screenshot editor page, and tap the checkmark icon in the top-right corner. Here, you can select "Copy and Delete" to save the screenshot to your clipboard and delete it from your device. You can now paste it in other apps, such as Mail, Messages, or WhatsApp. Goodbye, clutter.

Your iPhone comes with a powerful text extraction tool that lets you copy text from images. Just take a screenshot, tap the thumbnail in the bottom-left corner, and hit the Live Text button in the bottom-right corner. This tool instantly identifies all kinds of text in an image, and, from there, you can select and copy it easily.

When I'm annotating a screenshot, I'll often draw a quick squiggle to highlight something to others who'll view it. Since I'm no Picasso, my attempts at drawing a circle (or any other shape) over an element in the screenshot look hopelessly amateur. Fortunately, iOS has a feature that allows you to turn your squiggles into regular shapes. Try this: Draw your best estimation of a circle, rectangle, square, or another shape on a screenshot. Immediately after, hold the screen, and iOS will convert your drawing into a neat symmetrical shape.

I've seen way too many screenshots with poorly hidden bits of sensitive information. When people do this using an iPhone, they often use the pen tool or even the highlighter to hide email addresses, phone numbers, or names. It's surprisingly easy to bypass these methods for those in the know, leaving your info vulnerable. If you're trying to securely hide info in an image, use opaque shapes instead. It's a built-in tool on your iPhone that hides information thoroughly, and is much faster than scribbling over text hundreds of times. When you take a screenshot, open the image via its thumbnail, and tap the pen icon up top. Hit the + button in the bottom-right corner, and tap Add Shape. Choose any shape you like, and tap the first circle in the popover menu to add any color. This will make it an opaque shape. Now, drag this shape over sensitive information and save the image.

Deleting a bunch of screenshots by hand is a pain. However, you can use Apple's Shortcuts app to create an automation to do the job for you. The basic logic behind this automation is to find all photos that are screenshots taken in a specific time period, and delete them in one shot. For most people, this will work as a periodic cleanup tool that deletes recently taken screenshots. As an example, you can use it to delete all screenshots taken in the past 30 days. I've created a sample shortcut for you to follow. You can modify it to suit your needs, but if you use it as is, it'll find and delete all screenshots from the past month. It does ask for confirmation before deleting screenshots, and even after it's done, you can still recover photos from the Recently Deleted folder.

This might be how screenshots work on your iPhone: You take a screenshot, and the device shows a thumbnail in the bottom-left corner. This disappears in a few seconds, and saves the screenshot to your library. If you accidentally take a screenshot and don't tap the thumbnail fast enough, you'll have to manually delete the screenshot from your library. If this bothers you, then I recommend enabling full-screen screenshot previews. That way, the moment you take a screenshot (accidental or not), you'll see a preview, and you can decide if you want to keep the image.

Apple has since changed this default, so there's a chance your screenshots now open in full-screen already. However, if your iPhone is still running with the thumbnail method, you can set this up by going to Settings > General > Screen Capture and enabling Full-Screen Previews.

In addition to screenshots, you can take screen recordings of your iPhone as well. There are many uses for this, but one of the best is to create a screencast. I use this often to help my parents solve tech problems. You can also add microphone audio to these screencasts to make them even more useful, and to avoid recording a voiceover separately. To do this, open Control Center by swiping down from the top-right corner of the screen. In case you don't see the screen recording button here, you can add it by tapping the + button in the top-left corner, and selecting Add a Control > Screen Recording.

Hold the screen recording button until you see a pop-up menu. Tap the "Microphone Off" button, and it'll change to Microphone On. Tap Start Recording, wait for three seconds, and the screen recording will begin. You can now start speaking, and your voice will be a part of your screen recording.

If you want to take screenshots with maximum efficiency, try Screenshot, a screenshot shortcut I found on Reddit. This shortcut bypasses all screenshot previews and capture sounds, and instantly saves your screenshot to a library of your choice. Once you install this shortcut, review its steps, and select an album for your screenshot. (It drops your screenshots in the Recents album by default, which may not be ideal for everyone.) From here, open Control Center, tap the + button, select Add a Control > Shortcut. Now select the Screenshot shortcut, and you're good to go. The next time you want to capture a screenshot as fast as possible, run this shortcut from the Control Center, and you'll notice that it's the least intrusive screenshot workflow. You could even link this shortcut to Back Tap gestures for even faster access.

title: Here's How the Cameras on Google's New Pixel 11 Phones Compare to the iPhone
description: Google just dropped the specs on the new Pixel 11 cameras.
fullText:
Ahead of its annual Made by Google event in New York City, Google revealed the details of its upcoming line of Pixel 11 phones, including specs of their all-important cameras. Pixel 11 phones will come in three versions: the base Pixel 11, the Pixel 11 Pro, and the Pixel 11 Pro XL. The Pro and Pro XL cameras have the same features, while the base model sports a slightly scaled-down photographic system.

The standard Pixel 11's camera setup is a step up from the Pixel 10, but not a gigantic leap. The main improvement is the brighter main sensor; the lenses are close to last year's hardware. Here's how it breaks down:

Main: 48MP wide camera (rear) with a 1/1.56" sensor (larger than last year's model) to improve light input.

Ultrawide: 13MP, which is identical to the Pixel 10's ultrawide camera specs.

Telephoto: 10.8MP telephoto with 5X optical zoom and a 30x digital zoom. Also the same as the Pixel 10.

Front camera: 10.5MP, also identical to the Pixel 10.

Google is throwing the heavy hardware improvements into its pro-level phones, bumping up both the resolution and sensor sizes across almost every lens.

Main: 50MP wide camera, with a 1/1.3" sensor for improved light-gathering.

Ultrawide: 48MP ultrawide camera, a big leap from the 13MP ultrawide of the base model.

Telephoto: 48MP telephoto with 5X optical zoom and an "AI-powered" 120x Pro Zoom.

Front camera: The Pro's 42MP selfie camera is a big step up from the 10.5MP camera on the base Pixel 11.

With Apple's iPhones holding down over 50% of the U.S. smart phone market compared to Pixel's 3%, Google faces a real battle to win over buyers. Camera quality is a powerful weapon in its arsenal. Most consumers consider the camera an important choice when choosing between cell phones, and it's the most important feature for about half of younger users. Here's how Pixel 11's pro tier camera stacks up against the iPhone 17 Pro's best camera offerings.

Main sensor: The Pixel 11 Pro edges out Apple slightly with a 50MP lens compared to the iPhone 17 Pro's 48MP, but megapixels are more complex than just "more is better." Apple's main sensor is 1/1.28," which is slightly larger than the Pixel's 1/1.3" sensor, and sensor size is more important to low-light performance and dynamic range than raw pixels. So this one's closer to a wash than the megapixel numbers suggest.

Ultrawide: It's dead even. Both phones feature 48-megapixel ultrawide lenses.

Telephoto: When it comes to zooming, Google is slightly ahead, offering 5x zoom to Apple's 4x, but in terms of digital zoom, the Pixel 11 Pro's 120x zoom towers over Apple's 40x zoom—in a way. Google's "pro zoom" is built on generative AI, producing plausible details for things it can't see, leading to a realistic-looking photo. Apple's approach uses AI more modestly, focusing on stacking multiple exposures to reduce noise and fill in details. The end result: Apple's extreme zoom is more grainy and noisy, but also more real.

Front camera: The Pixel has a real advantage here with a 42MP sensor compared to Apple's 18MP selfie camera.

Both lines of smart phone cameras are roughly equal in terms of raw power. The main difference is largely a philosophical one. Apple might be losing the extreme magnification fight by capping its digital zoom to a relatively modest 40x, but it's also avoiding producing photos that are largely a product of artificial intelligence. If you want to push the boundaries of what a lens can capture with the help of generative AI, and you're not overly concerned about verisimilitude, the Pixel is the choice. If you want to keep it real (well, real-ish, anyway) the iPhone is the choice.

title: Five New Changes in iOS 27 Beta 5
description: Apple's latest test build of iOS 27 has some small but worthwhile updates.
fullText:
Apple released the fifth beta for iOS 27 on Monday, Aug. 10. As we get closer to the update's official fall release, the number of features and changes Apple will introduce with each beta is certainly diminishing, and no one would call beta 5 a feature-filled update. However, there are some new features and changes worth noting, especially as they are things Apple didn't previously announce at WWDC. 

Before I get into what's new, a reminder: iOS 27 is not yet finished. As such, while anyone with a compatible iPhone can install it, know there are risks to running beta software on your device. Make sure to make a proper backup of your data, as you could lose everything on your iPhone in the event you need to downgrade back to iOS 26.

When you update your iPhone to the latest iOS 27 beta—or, presumably, iOS 27 itself—you're going to notice new icons for some familiar apps. Some updates are quite subtle, such as Safari. You might not even notice at first, since the icon retains the same basic design as before, but with this latest beta, Safari now has fewer "ticks" in its compass than before, a slightly different blue background, and a distinct screw in its center. It reminds me a bit of iOS 7's flat design. It's the same story for Settings and the App Store icons: small adjustments that you might not notice without comparing the icons side by side.

If you've been running the beta, you'll notice the update to the Siri app right away. Instead of the colorful, looping logo Apple debuted with the app, Siri now appears as a gray, glowing orb. Preview's new app icon is also readily apparent: replacing the loupe against a blue background, the new logo places the loop in the bottom-right corner of a colorful, rounded square. I'm personally a fan of these changes, especially for Preview.

If you have a compatible iPhone, you can customize how Siri AI sounds through a new feature called "enhanced voice." With it, you can change both Siri's pace and expressivity to make a voice that's a bit more unique to your iPhone than others. With the first four iOS 27 betas, enhanced voice only worked with various American English accents. But starting with iOS 27 beta 5, Apple now supports customizing British English voices as well. According to 9to5Mac, you now have 11 different voices to customize.

Dive into the Settings after updating your iPhone, and you'll find a new option in the "Search Settings" menu. "Before Searching" comes with three new settings. The biggest change is "Suggest Apps," which lets you choose how many suggested apps appear in Siri Suggestions (the default is eight). There's also "Suggest App Shortcuts," which appears to let you choose whether or not iOS suggests app shortcuts, and "Show Recent Searches," which lets you hide your searches from this menu.

As reported by Apple Insider, iOS 27 beta 5 will tell you when you installed your current version of iOS on your iPhone. I'm not sure exactly in what scenarios this would be useful, but it's a new change.

Here's a small but interesting change: Apple is no longer showing cellular network types while you're on wifi. If you check Control Center, you won't see whether you're connected to LTE, 5G, or something like 5G UWB as long as you're connected to wifi as well. You'll need to jump off the wifi to see what cellular network your iPhone is connected to. (For what it's worth, I currently can't see my cellular network type while connected to wifi on iOS 26 either, but maybe that's a carrier thing, as I'm seeing multiple reports about this change.)

(Bloomberg) -- Apple Inc.'s Jennifer Bailey, the longtime head of Pay and Wallet services, is retiring after more than two decades at the company, adding to a sweeping changing of the guard at the iPhone maker.
